Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Fungal class D1 G-protein-coupled receptor that acts as an alpha-factor pheromone receptor performing pheromone-dependent signal transduction involved in cellular conjugation, mating projection assembly, and in cell fusion (PubMed:10744981, PubMed:11495900, PubMed:12427030, PubMed:2556384, PubMed:2839507, PubMed:2842059, PubMed:3023832, PubMed:3037311, PubMed:4595644, PubMed:6353246, PubMed:6360378, PubMed:6993497, PubMed:9286665, PubMed:9529386, PubMed:9742115, PubMed:9819407, PubMed:9824658). Following alpha-factor-binding, the signal is transmitted via a tripartite G protein consisting of alpha-, beta- and gamma-subunits (GAP1, STE4 and STE8 respectively) that prepares the cell for conjugation (PubMed:10866688, PubMed:11287148, PubMed:1330324, PubMed:1647971, PubMed:8132618, PubMed:8385135, PubMed:8692892). In the inactive state, the cytoplasmic end of transmembrane domain 7 (TMD7) is unstructured and packs between TMD1-6, blocking the G protein coupling site (PubMed:35296853). FUNCTION: Component of the ribosome, a large ribonucleoprotein complex responsible for the synthesis of proteins in the cell. The small ribosomal subunit (SSU) binds messenger RNAs (mRNAs) and translates the encoded message by selecting cognate aminoacyl-transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules. The large subunit (LSU) contains the ribosomal catalytic site termed the peptidyl transferase center (PTC), which catalyzes the formation of peptide bonds, thereby polymerizing the amino acids delivered by tRNAs into a polypeptide chain. The nascent polypeptides leave the ribosome through a tunnel in the LSU and interact with protein factors that function in enzymatic processing, targeting, and the membrane insertion of nascent chains at the exit of the ribosomal tunnel (PubMed:22096102). uS4 is involved in nucleolar processing of pre-18S ribosomal RNA and ribosome assembly (PubMed:15590835). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:15590835, ECO:0000305|PubMed:22096102}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Component the THO subcomplex of the TREX complex, which operates in coupling transcription elongation to mRNA export. The THO complex is recruited to transcribed genes and moves along the gene with the elongating polymerase during transcription. THO is important for stabilizing nascent RNA in the RNA polymerase II elongation complex by preventing formation of DNA:RNA hybrids behind the elongating polymerase. It functions in cotranscriptional formation of an export-competent messenger ribonucleoprotein particle (mRNP) by facilitating the loading of ATP-dependent RNA helicase SUB2 and the mRNA export factor YRA1 along the nascent mRNA. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:12093753, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12871933, ECO:0000269|PubMed:14527416, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15192704}.

FUNCTION: Transcriptional coactivator that stimulates GCN4-dependent transcriptional activity by bridging the DNA-binding region of GCN4 and TBP (SPT15), thereby recruiting TBP to GCN4-bound promoters (PubMed:9710580). Involved in induction of the ribosome quality control (RQC) pathway; a pathway that degrades nascent peptide chains during problematic translation (PubMed:30465652, PubMed:36583309). Required to prevent stalled ribosomes from frameshifting (PubMed:30465652, PubMed:36583309). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:30465652, ECO:0000269|PubMed:36583309, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9710580}.

FUNCTION: Involved in mitochondrial distribution and morphology. Mediates the import of UPS1, UPS2 and UPS3, 3 atypical mitochondrial intermembrane space (IMS) proteins lacking the two major IMS-targeting signals, into the intermembrane space. The UPS1:MDM35 complex mediates the transfer of phosphatidic acid (PA) between liposomes and probably functions as a PA transporter across the mitochondrion intermembrane space (PubMed:26071601, PubMed:26071602, PubMed:26235513). Phosphatidic acid import is required for cardiolipin (CL) synthesis in the mitochondrial inner membrane (PubMed:26071602). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11907266, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20622808, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20657548, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26071601, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26071602, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26235513}.

FUNCTION: Mitochondrial intermembrane chaperone that participates in the import and insertion of multi-pass transmembrane proteins into the mitochondrial inner membrane. Also required for the transfer of beta-barrel precursors from the TOM complex to the sorting and assembly machinery (SAM complex) of the outer membrane. Acts as a chaperone-like protein that protects the hydrophobic precursors from aggregation and guide them through the mitochondrial intermembrane space. FUNCTION: Versatile protein that might stabilize multiple protein complexes involved in diverse pathways. Subunit of the 26S proteasome which plays a role in ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis. Also associates with the TREX-2 complex that is required for transcription-coupled mRNA export, and the COP9 signalosome, which is involved in deneddylation. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:15117943, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19289793}.

FUNCTION: Electron carrier protein. The oxidized form of the cytochrome c heme group can accept an electron from the heme group of the cytochrome c1 subunit of ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase. Cytochrome c then transfers this electron to the dinuclear copper A center (CU(A)) of the COX2 subunit of cytochrome oxidase, the final protein carrier in the mitochondrial electron-transport chain. Isoform 1 (CYC1) is the predominant cytochrome c during aerobic/normoxic growth. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:7814361, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7851399, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9169434}.

FUNCTION: Component of the ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase, a multisubunit transmembrane complex that is part of the mitochondrial electron transport chain which drives oxidative phosphorylation. The respiratory chain contains 3 multisubunit complexes succinate dehydrogenase (complex II, CII), ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase (cytochrome b-c1 complex, complex III, CIII) and cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV, CIV), that cooperate to transfer electrons derived from NADH and succinate to molecular oxygen, creating an electrochemical gradient over the inner membrane that drives transmembrane transport and the ATP synthase. The cytochrome b-c1 complex catalyzes electron transfer from ubiquinol to cytochrome c, linking this redox reaction to translocation of protons across the mitochondrial inner membrane, with protons being carried across the membrane as hydrogens on the quinol. In the process called Q cycle, 2 protons are consumed from the matrix, 4 protons are released into the intermembrane space and 2 electrons are passed to cytochrome c. {ECO:0000250|UniProtKB:P07919, ECO:0000305|PubMed:11880631}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Component of the cytochrome c oxidase, the last enzyme in the mitochondrial electron transport chain which drives oxidative phosphorylation. The respiratory chain contains 3 multisubunit complexes succinate dehydrogenase (complex II, CII), ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase (cytochrome b-c1 complex, complex III, CIII) and cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV, CIV), that cooperate to transfer electrons derived from NADH and succinate to molecular oxygen, creating an electrochemical gradient over the inner membrane that drives transmembrane transport and the ATP synthase. Cytochrome c oxidase is the component of the respiratory chain that catalyzes the reduction of oxygen to water. Electrons originating from reduced cytochrome c in the intermembrane space (IMS) are transferred via the dinuclear copper A center (CU(A)) of COX2 and heme A of COX1 to the active site in COX1, a binuclear center (BNC) formed by heme A3 and copper B (CU(B)). The BNC reduces molecular oxygen to 2 water molecules using 4 electrons from cytochrome c in the IMS and 4 protons from the mitochondrial matrix (Probable). COX1 is a catalytic core subunit containing heme A and the active site BNC with heme A3 and the copper atom CU(B) (PubMed:30598554). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:30598554, ECO:0000305|PubMed:30598554}.

Merged_Functions: CDC19 is described as a housekeeping gene that encodes pyruvate kinase, a metabolic enzyme of key importance to the yeast cell cycle. It functions in central metabolism, catalyzing the final step of glycolysis and thereby contributing critically to energy production and cell‑cycle progression in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. {PubMed:16879422}. CDC19 encodes pyruvate kinase, a key enzyme of the glycolytic pathway that catalyzes the conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate, linking glycolysis to the pyruvate‑to‑ethanol pathway. In the study, CDC19 expression was significantly up‑regulated during high‑temperature ethanol fermentation, suggesting that increased pyruvate kinase activity contributes to enhanced ethanol production under stress conditions. {PubMed:28721580}. CDC19 encodes the pyruvate kinase enzyme that catalyzes the final step of glycolysis, converting phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate with a net production of two ATP molecules. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, CDC19 activity is linked to cell‑division cycle progression (temperature‑sensitive cdc19 mutants arrest in G1 at elevated temperatures) and, as shown in this study, higher pyruvate kinase activity (due to specific silent mutations in the CDC19 allele) contributes to the dominant high‑temperature growth (Htg⁺) phenotype. The increased enzymatic activity enhances energy metabolism, supporting cellular homeostasis under heat stress, although it does not alter CDC19 transcription levels. {PubMed:21459167}. CDC19 encodes the major isoform of yeast pyruvate kinase, a key glycolytic enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of phosphoenol‑pyruvate (PEP) to pyruvate, thereby driving ATP production and providing building blocks for biosynthesis. In addition to its metabolic role, CDC19 participates in stress adaptation: under glucose starvation or other stresses it undergoes reversible, amyloid‑like aggregation mediated by a low‑complexity region (LCR). This aggregation is regulated by oligomeric state, allosteric binding of fructose‑1,6‑bisphosphate (FBP), and phosphorylation of the LCR. Aggregated CDC19 localizes to Pab1‑positive stress granules, where it is protected from degradation, enabling rapid re‑solubilization and restoration of glycolytic flux when favorable conditions return, thus facilitating cell‑cycle re‑entry after stress. {PubMed:28846094}. CDC19 encodes the major pyruvate kinase enzyme (Pyk1p) that catalyzes the irreversible conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) to pyruvate, a key step in the glycolytic pathway and thus central to carbohydrate metabolism. In the context of this study, CDC19 expression was down‑regulated as very‑high‑gravity ethanol fermentation progressed, indicating a slowdown of glucose catabolism under high ethanol concentrations and suggesting that its role in thermal stress response reported elsewhere did not contribute to ethanol tolerance under the examined conditions. {PubMed:23625881}. CDC19 encodes the principal isoform of pyruvate kinase in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. It catalyzes the final, essentially irreversible step of glycolysis, converting phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate, and is essential for fermentative growth. The enzyme is allosterically activated by fructose‑1,6‑bisphosphate. CDC19 is a major hub for post‑translational regulation: it is phosphorylated by protein kinase A (PKA) on Ser22, which stimulates its activity; it is also extensively modified by lysine acetylation (19 sites) and ubiquitination (23 sites), indicating additional layers of control over its activity and stability. {PubMed:25512067}. PYK1 (encoded by CDC19) is the pyruvate kinase that catalyzes the final step of glycolysis, converting phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate with the concomitant production of ATP. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae it plays a role in the cell‑division cycle and is essential for normal growth. HIS4 encodes an essential enzyme required for the biosynthesis of histidine in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. {PubMed:2407614}. The YCL183 gene (referred to in the article as SPT14) encodes an essential 50 kDa protein that functions as a positive transcriptional regulator in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Unlike the related SPT13/GAL11 gene, SPT14 does not significantly affect GAL4‑regulated genes.  Overall, SPT14/YCL183 is an essential transcriptional activator that specifically promotes expression of Ty elements, HIS4, and a subset of mating‑type genes. {PubMed:1660567}. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Mitochondrial membrane ATP synthase (F(1)F(0) ATP synthase or Complex V) produces ATP from ADP in the presence of a proton gradient across the membrane which is generated by electron transport complexes of the respiratory chain. F-type ATPases consist of two structural domains, F(1) - containing the extramembraneous catalytic core, and F(0) - containing the membrane proton channel, linked together by a central stalk and a peripheral stalk. During catalysis, ATP synthesis in the catalytic domain of F(1) is coupled via a rotary mechanism of the central stalk subunits to proton translocation. Subunits alpha and beta form the catalytic core in F(1). Rotation of the central stalk against the surrounding alpha(3)beta(3) subunits leads to hydrolysis of ATP in three separate catalytic sites on the beta subunits.

The gene contains multiple cis‑acting regulatory elements (Gcr1p‑binding motifs, UAS1/UAS2 sites, Rap1p, Ebf1p, Abf1p) that mediate glucose‑dependent induction. ENO2 protein can form homo‑ and heterodimers with ENO1‑encoded enolase, contributing to the pool of active enolase dimers. Besides its central metabolic role, ENO2 (like ENO1) has been implicated in non‑glycolytic functions such as mitochondrial tRNA import and vacuole formation, although these additional roles are not the primary focus of the article. {PubMed:23359425}. ENO2 encodes enolase II, an enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of 2‑phosphoglycerate to phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) in the glycolytic pathway. In this study, overexpression of ENO2 was used to increase the cellular supply of PEP, thereby enhancing flux toward the L‑tyrosine biosynthetic pathway and improving p‑coumaric acid production. {PubMed:32550099}. ENO2 encodes an mRNA whose abundance and translation are strongly affected by heat stress in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Upon severe heat stress (46 °C for 10 min) the ENO2 transcript level drops dramatically, and its translational activity is reduced in wild‑type cells. Deletion of TPK2 further diminishes the heat‑induced translational repression of ENO2, whereas deletion of TPK3 does not produce a noticeable change in ENO2 translational activity compared with wild type. Thus, ENO2 serves as a heat‑stress‑responsive gene whose expression is modulated at both the transcriptional and translational levels. {PubMed:29045428}.

Is transcriptionally and translationally repressed during heat stress; heat‑induced translational repression is enhanced by TPK2 deletion. {PubMed:29045428}. Merged_Functions: The TRP3 gene of Saccharomyces cerevisiae encodes a bifunctional enzyme that participates in tryptophan biosynthesis. Its N‑terminal region functions as a glutamine amidotransferase, supplying the amidogenic glutamine‑derived nitrogen required by the anthranilate synthase (TRP2) complex (“aggregation region”). The C‑terminal region possesses indole‑3‑glycerol‑phosphate synthase (InGP‑synthase) activity, which can act independently of TRP2. Consequently, the TRP3 protein is organized as NH₂‑glutamine amidotransferase‑InGP‑synthase‑COOH and is essential for the synthesis of indole‑3‑glycerol‑phosphate, a precursor in the tryptophan pathway, as well as for providing glutamine‑derived ammonia to the TRP2‑TRP3 enzyme complex. {PubMed:24177735}. The TRP3 gene of *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* encodes a bifunctional peptide that carries two independent catalytic activities required for tryptophan biosynthesis. The N‑terminal region (approximately 600–700 bp) provides a glutamine amidotransferase activity, which supplies the ammonia needed for the anthranilate synthase (TRP2) complex (“aggregation region”). The C‑terminal region (approximately 900 bp) encodes an indole‑3‑glycerol‑phosphate synthase (InGP‑synthase) activity, catalyzing the conversion of the appropriate intermediate in the tryptophan pathway. Together, a contiguous DNA fragment of about 1.5 kb contains both functions, but each domain can function autonomously when expressed separately, as demonstrated by deletion and complementation analyses. {PubMed:24177736}. TRP3 encodes the N‑terminal portion of the bifunctional tryptophan‑biosynthetic enzyme found in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. According to the article, this gene provides the glutamine amidotransferase activity (the first step of the pathway) and the indole‑3‑glycerol‑phosphate synthase (InGP‑synthase) activity (the fourth step of the pathway). Thus, TRP3 is essential for two consecutive reactions that convert chorismic acid toward tryptophan. The gene retains a conserved upstream promoter consensus sequence that mediates its response to the general control regulatory system, although its derepression is modest compared with TRP1. {PubMed:2998296}. The TRP3 gene encodes indole‑3‑glycerol‑phosphate synthase (EC 4.1.1.48), the enzyme that catalyzes the cyclization step in the tryptophan biosynthetic pathway, converting 1‑(2′‑carboxyphenylamino)‑1‑deoxyribulose‑5‑phosphate into indole‑3‑glycerol‑phosphate. This enzyme functions independently of its association with the anthranilate synthase complex (the TRP2 gene product) and is required for the synthesis of tryptophan. Mutations in TRP3 affect indole‑3‑glycerol‑phosphate synthase activity (trp3B), anthranilate synthase activity (trp3C), or both (trp3A), and the cloned 5.2 kb BamHI fragment containing TRP3 complements all three mutation types, confirming that it carries the full structural and regulatory sequences necessary for normal enzyme production and regulation by the general control system. {PubMed:24186086}. TRP3 encodes indole‑3‑glycerol‑phosphate synthase, an enzyme that catalyzes a key step in the de novo synthesis of tryptophan in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. In the study, TRP3 was disrupted as part of a “push‑pull‑restrain” strategy to limit flux through the tryptophan biosynthetic pathway, thereby redirecting carbon toward the engineered tyrosol and salidroside production routes. {PubMed:32369184}.

FUNCTION: Molecular chaperone that promotes the maturation, structural maintenance and proper regulation of specific target proteins involved in cell cycle control and signal transduction. Undergoes a functional cycle that is linked to its ATPase activity. FUNCTION: Part of the plasmid amplification system, which corrects any decrease in copy number caused by a rare missegregation event. FUNCTION: Part of the plasmid partitioning system, which ensures the equal distribution of replicated plasmid molecules to daughter cells. REP1-REP2 stably associate with CSE4-containing chromatin at STB during S-phase, marking the locus with a centromeric tag, and thereby probably catching mitotic spindle microtubules to the plasmid cluster and coupling plasmid segregation to chromosome segregation. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates. Largest and catalytic component of RNA polymerase II which synthesizes mRNA precursors and many functional non-coding RNAs. Forms the polymerase active center together with the second largest subunit. Pol II is the central component of the basal RNA polymerase II transcription machinery. During a transcription cycle, Pol II, general transcription factors and the Mediator complex assemble as the preinitiation complex (PIC) at the promoter. 11-15 base pairs of DNA surrounding the transcription start site are melted and the single-stranded DNA template strand of the promoter is positioned deeply within the central active site cleft of Pol II to form the open complex. After synthesis of about 30 bases of RNA, Pol II releases its contacts with the core promoter and the rest of the transcription machinery (promoter clearance) and enters the stage of transcription elongation in which it moves on the template as the transcript elongates. Pol II appears to oscillate between inactive and active conformations at each step of nucleotide addition. Elongation is influenced by the phosphorylation status of the C-terminal domain (CTD) of Pol II largest subunit (RPB1), which serves as a platform for assembly of factors that regulate transcription initiation, elongation, termination and mRNA processing. Pol II is composed of mobile elements that move relative to each other. The core element with the central large cleft comprises RPB3, RBP10, RPB11, RPB12 and regions of RPB1 and RPB2 forming the active center. The clamp element (portions of RPB1, RPB2 and RPB3) is connected to the core through a set of flexible switches and moves to open and close the cleft. A bridging helix emanates from RPB1 and crosses the cleft near the catalytic site and is thought to promote translocation of Pol II by acting as a ratchet that moves the RNA-DNA hybrid through the active site by switching from straight to bent conformations at each step of nucleotide addition. In elongating Pol II, the lid loop (RPB1) appears to act as a wedge to drive apart the DNA and RNA strands at the upstream end of the transcription bubble and guide the RNA strand toward the RNA exit groove located near the base of the largely unstructured CTD domain of RPB1. The rudder loop (RPB1) interacts with single-stranded DNA after separation from the RNA strand, likely preventing reassociation with the exiting RNA. The cleft is surrounded by jaws: an upper jaw formed by portions of RBP1, RPB2 and RPB9, and a lower jaw, formed by RPB5 and portions of RBP1. The jaws are thought to grab the incoming DNA template, mainly by RPB5 direct contacts to DNA.

APS1 (yeast YPR011c) encodes a mitochondrial carrier protein that mediates the exchange of adenosine 5'-phosphosulfate (APS) and 3'-phosphoadenosine 5'-phosphosulfate (PAPS) across the inner mitochondrial membrane. The transporter also moves sulfate, phosphate, thiosulfate and pyrosulfate, but shows the highest affinity for APS and PAPS. By exporting mitochondrial‑produced APS to the cytosol, APS1 supports sulfur assimilation pathways that generate methionine and glutathione, especially during thermal stress (45 °C). Loss of APS1 reduces thermotolerance, methionine content, and total glutathione levels, indicating its crucial role in heat‑shock survival and sulfur metabolism. {PubMed:24296033}. APS1 encodes Aps1p, a small (≈18 kDa) subunit homologous to the σ1 subunit of the mammalian AP‑1 clathrin‑associated protein complex. Aps1p is a peripheral membrane protein that forms part of high‑molecular‑weight AP‑like complexes distinct from those containing the related Aps2p. It co‑fractionates with clathrin‑coated vesicles and its association with these vesicles is lost in cells lacking clathrin, indicating that Aps1p interacts directly or indirectly with clathrin at the Golgi apparatus. Although deletion of APS1 alone produces no obvious phenotype, loss of APS1 aggravates growth defects of temperature‑sensitive or null clathrin heavy‑chain mutants and enhances the α‑factor maturation defect caused by compromised clathrin, suggesting that Aps1p contributes to a subset of clathrin‑dependent processes at the Golgi, likely involving retention of the Kex2p protease required for α‑factor processing. Additionally, APS1 deletion further impairs growth of cells completely lacking clathrin, implying that Aps1p also participates in clathrin‑independent functions. Overall, APS1 functions as a component of an AP‑1–like complex that modulates clathrin‑mediated vesicle formation and cargo sorting at the Golgi and may have additional clathrin‑independent roles. {PubMed:8157009}. APS1 encodes a MutT/Nudix motif hydrolase in Schizosaccharomyces pombe that efficiently hydrolyzes diadenosine polyphosphates, especially Ap₆A and Ap₅A, converting them into lower‑phosphate products (e.g., AMP, ADP, p₅A, p₄A, ATP). In addition, APS1 can act on diphosphorylated inositol polyphosphates, cleaving the β‑phosphate from PP‑InsP₅ to produce InsP₆ and also hydrolyzing [PP]₂‑InsP₄. Thus, APS1 functions as a dual‑specificity phosphohydrolase that regulates cellular levels of both diadenosine polyphosphates and diphosphoinositol polyphosphates. {PubMed:10419486}. Encodes a plastid‑targeted ATP‑sulfurylase that catalyzes the first committed step of sulfate assimilation in Arabidopsis thaliana, converting ATP and inorganic sulfate into adenosine‑5′‑phosphosulfate (APS) and pyrophosphate. This activation of sulfate enables downstream synthesis of cysteine, methionine, glutathione and other sulfated metabolites. APS1 is the most highly expressed member of the three‑gene ATP‑sulfurylase family and can functionally complement a yeast met3 (ATP‑sulfurylase) mutant, demonstrating its essential role in sulfate activation. {PubMed:7487067}. APS1 encodes the chloroplast form of ATP sulfurylase in Arabidopsis thaliana. The enzyme catalyzes the first step of the plant sulfate assimilation pathway by converting ATP and inorganic sulfate into adenosine 5'-phosphosulfate (APS), thereby activating sulfate for subsequent metabolic reactions such as reduction to sulfide for cysteine biosynthesis or transfer to hydroxyl or carbon groups for sulfation of proteins, peptides, oligosaccharides, flavonoids, and sulfolipids. Expression of APS1 complements a yeast met3 mutant, confirming its functional ATP sulfurylase activity. {PubMed:8058839}. APS1 encodes one of the three originally identified Arabidopsis thaliana ATP sulfurylase isoforms. Like the other isoforms, APS1 is predicted to be localized to plastids (chloroplasts) and to catalyze the first step of the sulfate assimilation pathway: the ATP‑dependent activation of inorganic sulfate to form 5′‑adenylylsulfate (APS) and pyrophosphate. The ARG3 gene encodes the enzyme ornithine carbamoyltransferase (OTCase, EC 2.1.3.3), which catalyzes the transfer of a carbamoyl group from carbamoyl‑phosphate to ornithine, producing citrulline as part of the arginine biosynthetic pathway in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The gene’s promoter and leader sequences have been examined, showing that neither the conserved central box in the operator nor the short leader RNA sequence is essential for this repression. {PubMed:2897249}. The arg3 gene of *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* encodes ornithine carbamoyltransferase (OrnCarbTase, EC 2.1.3.3), the enzyme that transfers a carbamoyl group from carbamoyl‑phosphate to L‑ornithine, a crucial step in the arginine biosynthetic pathway. The gene is subject to a specific negative regulatory mechanism: its expression is repressed by arginine (and fully repressed when both arginine and ornithine are present). In addition, it participates in the general control of amino‑acid synthesis that depends on tRNA aminoacylation levels. The cloned arg3 retains normal regulatory responses in yeast, shows arginine‑dependent repression, and can be affected by cis‑dominant regulatory mutations that alter its control region. Native arg3 does not produce functional enzyme in *E. coli* unless secondary mutations create a weak promoter, allowing low‑level expression of the yeast OrnCarbTase in the bacterial host. {PubMed:7029528}. ARG3 is an arginine biosynthetic (anabolic) gene whose transcription is subject to arginine‑dependent repression. Sequences upstream of ARG3 that are required for this repression share homology with the CAR1 UAS_I elements and can substitute for those elements in reporter assays, indicating that ARG3 expression is negatively regulated by arginine through specific upstream regulatory sequences. {PubMed:1400233}. The ARG3 gene encodes the monomeric subunit of the trimeric enzyme ornithine carbamoyltransferase (OTCase, EC 2.1.3.3). OTCase catalyzes the sixth step of the arginine biosynthetic pathway, converting carbamoyl phosphate and ornithine into citrulline during the synthesis of arginine from glutamate. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae the enzyme is cytosolic and functions anabolically. Its activity is regulated by formation of a complex with the catabolic enzyme arginase, which prevents wasteful recycling of ornithine when arginine is used as a nitrogen source. {PubMed:3038540}.

The large subunit (LSU) contains the ribosomal catalytic site termed the peptidyl transferase center (PTC), which catalyzes the formation of peptide bonds, thereby polymerizing the amino acids delivered by tRNAs into a polypeptide chain. The nascent polypeptides leave the ribosome through a tunnel in the LSU and interact with protein factors that function in enzymatic processing, targeting, and the membrane insertion of nascent chains at the exit of the ribosomal tunnel. {ECO:0000305|PubMed:22096102}.

FUNCTION: [Ubiquitin]: Exists either covalently attached to another protein, or free (unanchored). When covalently bound, it is conjugated to target proteins via an isopeptide bond either as a monomer (monoubiquitin), a polymer linked via different Lys residues of the ubiquitin (polyubiquitin chains) or a linear polymer linked via the initiator Met of the ubiquitin (linear polyubiquitin chains). Polyubiquitin chains, when attached to a target protein, have different functions depending on the Lys residue of the ubiquitin that is linked: Lys-6-linked may be involved in DNA repair; Lys-11-linked is involved in ERAD (endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation) and in cell-cycle regulation; Lys-29-linked is involved in lysosomal degradation; Lys-33-linked is involved in kinase modification; Lys-48-linked is involved in protein degradation via the proteasome; Lys-63-linked is involved in endocytosis, and DNA-damage responses. Linear polymer chains formed via attachment by the initiator Met lead to cell signaling. Ubiquitin is usually conjugated to Lys residues of target proteins, however, in rare cases, conjugation to Cys or Ser residues has been observed. Merged_Functions: TPK3 encodes one of the three catalytic subunits of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase (PKA) in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. In this study, Tpk3 is shown to be specifically required for the hyper‑phosphorylation of the transcription factor Rgt1 under high‑glucose conditions. This Tpk3‑mediated hyper‑phosphorylation causes Rgt1 to dissociate from the HXK2 promoter, allowing HXK2 gene expression. Deletion of TPK3 prevents Rgt1 hyper‑phosphorylation, resulting in continued Rgt1 binding to the promoter even in high glucose, and thus impairs the normal glucose‑dependent regulation of HXK2. {PubMed:16528100}. TPK3 encodes one of the three catalytic subunits of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase A (PKA) in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.  While the three Tpk isoforms are individually dispensable for viability, Tpk3 has specific regulatory roles.  According to the study, Tpk3 (together with Tpk2) exerts an inhibitory effect on the TPK1 promoter, helping to maintain a repressive chromatin conformation and preventing the heat‑shock‑induced up‑regulation of TPK1.  Unlike TPK1, the TPK3 promoter is not activated by heat or osmotic stress.  Tpk3 protein is also reported to associate with processing bodies (PBs) during stationary phase, glucose starvation and hyper‑osmotic stress, reflecting a stress‑dependent subcellular localization.  Overall, Tpk3 contributes to the autoregulatory network that fine‑tunes PKA signaling specificity by repressing transcription of other PKA subunit genes under normal and stress conditions. {PubMed:32599085}. TPK3 encodes one of the three catalytic subunits (Tpk1, Tpk2, Tpk3) of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase (PKA) in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. In the experiments described, a strain that expresses only Tpk3 shows invertase (SUC2) activity that is similar to wild‑type, with the non‑induced (basal) level being slightly higher than in the wild‑type strain. This indicates that Tpk3 can support normal SUC2 expression and contributes to the PKA‑mediated regulation of invertase levels, particularly during growth on lactate with low glucose. The study concludes that Tpk3, together with the other Tpk isoforms, participates in the control of SUC2 transcription, but no unique role for Tpk3 beyond this general contribution is identified. {PubMed:25810078}. TPK3 encodes one of the three catalytic subunits of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase A (PKA) in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. In the context of heat stress, Tpk3 has a distinct role in the translational response: under mild heat stress (37 °C, 30 min) Tpk3 aggregates into cytoplasmic foci that co‑accumulate translation initiation factors eIF4G, Pab1 and eIF4E, and this aggregation depends on translation inhibition. Under severe heat stress (46 °C, 10 min) Tpk3 relocates to stress granules (SGs) and processing bodies (PBs) together with Tpk2 and components of a 48S pre‑initiation complex. Deletion of TPK3 suppresses the formation of SGs/PBs, diminishes translational arrest, and alters the translational regulation of specific mRNAs (e.g., CYC1, HSP30, HSP42, ENO2) during heat stress. Thus, Tpk3 functions as a promoter of translational repression and stress‑granule assembly during thermal stress, contributing to proper adaptation of the translational machinery. {PubMed:29045428}. TPK3 encodes one of the three catalytic subunits of the yeast cAMP‑dependent protein kinase (cAPK). As a catalytic subunit, Tpk3 can phosphorylate normal cAPK substrates such as the regulatory subunit (R) and downstream targets like fructose‑1,6‑bisphosphatase (FruP₂ase) when active. However, in wild‑type cells the TPK3 gene is expressed at a very low level, resulting in barely detectable Tpk3 protein and consequently minimal cAPK activity both in vitro (e.g., on kemptide) and in vivo (e.g., glucose‑induced FruP₂ase inactivation). Overexpression of TPK3 from a high‑copy plasmid or from the GAL1 promoter increases TPK3 mRNA, but high catalytic activity is only achieved when the regulatory subunit gene BCY1 is co‑overexpressed, indicating that excess R is required for efficient Tpk3 activity. Thus, the primary function of TPK3 is to serve as a catalytic component of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase complex, but its physiological impact is limited by its low transcriptional expression. {PubMed:8386630}. TPK3 encodes one of the three catalytic subunits of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase (PKA) in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. According to the article, increased RAS2 activity raises intracellular cAMP levels, which in turn activates the cAMP‑dependent protein kinases TPK1p, TPK2p, and TPK3p, leading to the breakdown of storage carbohydrates. The study also tested multicopy TPK3 as a potential suppressor of PPS1 overexpression–induced growth arrest and found that overexpression of TPK3 did not suppress this phenotype, indicating that TPK3 functions downstream of Ras2/cAMP signaling but is not directly involved in the PPS1‑related pathway. {PubMed:9083070}. TPK3 encodes one of the three catalytic subunits (Tpk1‑3) of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase (PKA) in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. In the context of this study, Tpk3 participates in the glucose‑ and Ras‑induced inhibition of the anaphase‑promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C). The three Tpk proteins have overlapping (redundant) functions for transmitting the signal from elevated cAMP/PKA activity to APC/C, such that deletion of TPK3 alone or together with another TPK gene does not prevent APC/C inhibition by glucose. However, under normal expression levels Tpk3 is less efficient than Tpk2 at mediating this inhibition, likely due to its lower catalytic activity and lower expression. When overexpressed from a high‑copy plasmid, Tpk3 becomes as effective as Tpk2 in blocking the viability of APC/C mutant strains, indicating that increased Tpk3 activity can strongly inhibit APC/C. Thus, Tpk3 functions as a catalytic subunit of PKA that can, redundantly with Tpk1 and Tpk2, mediate glucose‑ and Ras‑dependent inhibition of APC/C activity, with a comparatively lower intrinsic efficiency that can be overcome by overexpression. {PubMed:12724382}. TPK3 encodes one of the three catalytic subunits of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase (cAPK/PKA) in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.  The TPK genes (TPK1, TPK2, TPK3) produce homologous catalytic proteins that, together with the regulatory subunit BCY1, form the holoenzyme responsible for cAMP‑mediated phosphorylation events.  Although deletion of all three TPK genes is lethal, a single functional TPK allele can support normal growth.  Experimental data in the article show that strains retaining TPK3 (but lacking TPK1 and TPK2) exhibit reduced but detectable heat‑induced thermotolerance and trehalose accumulation, indicating that the TPK3‑encoded catalytic subunit contributes to the stress‑induced activation of PKA that is independent of changes in intracellular cAMP levels.  Thus, TPK3 is required for the full expression of cAMP‑independent, stress‑activated thermotolerance and participates in the regulation of trehalose synthesis during sublethal heat stress. {PubMed:1336794}. TPK3 encodes the catalytic subunit Tpk3 of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase A (PKA) in *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*.  In exponentially growing cells Tpk3 associates with translation initiation factors such as Pab1 and the small‑ribosomal protein Rps3, likely via the 48S pre‑initiation complex.  Upon glucose starvation this interaction is lost and Tpk3 relocalises to cytoplasmic RNA granules, first accumulating in processing bodies (PBs) and later also in stress granules (SGs).  The kinase activity of Tpk3 is required for its recruitment to pre‑formed PBs.  Deletion of TPK3 uncouples translational arrest from granule formation: cells lacking Tpk3 form abnormal granules even in the presence of glucose, fail to store mRNAs (e.g., ENO2) efficiently in PBs, and display altered granule composition (presence of Rpg1 and Rps3).  Moreover, TPK3 deletion leads to increased protein levels of the cap‑binding factor eIF4G1 and the eIF3 subunit Rpg1 during stationary phase, which correlates with a reduced ability to inhibit translation and a faster translational recovery when glucose is re‑added.  Overall, Tpk3 functions as a regulator that links nutrient signalling to the control of translation initiation, mRNA storage, and the dynamics of PB/SG assembly. {PubMed:22899713}. YKL166C (named PPS1) encodes a dual‑specificity protein phosphatase that contains an active C‑terminal phosphatase domain and an inactive phosphatase‑like domain. The enzyme dephosphorylates phosphotyrosyl and phosphothreonyl residues in synthetic peptides and can inactivate human MAP kinase ERK1. PPS1 transcript levels peak during early S phase, and the protein is proposed to maintain the DNA synthesis phase of the cell cycle by keeping a yet‑unknown substrate in a dephosphorylated state; overexpression of PPS1 leads to synchronous growth arrest and abnormal DNA replication, indicating that its normal activity is required for proper exit from S phase. Deletion of the gene produces no obvious phenotype, suggesting redundancy, but the phosphatase activity is essential for the overexpression phenotype. PPS1 function appears to intersect with the RAS2 signaling pathway, as multicopy RAS2 suppresses the growth arrest caused by PPS1 overexpression. {PubMed:9083070}. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, PKA3 (encoded by TPK3) is one of the three catalytic subunits of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase (PKA). The article shows that the Tpk3 subunit is specifically required for hyper‑phosphorylation of the transcription factor Rgt1 when cells are shifted to high‑glucose conditions. This hyper‑phosphorylation by Tpk3 (or a Tpk3‑dependent kinase) causes Rgt1 to dissociate from its binding site in the HXK2 promoter, thereby relieving repression and permitting HXK2 transcription. Deletion of TPK3 abolishes Rgt1 hyper‑phosphorylation and maintains Rgt1 binding to the promoter even in high glucose, but does not itself alter HXK2 expression levels. Thus, PKA3 functions as the glucose‑responsive catalytic subunit of PKA that mediates Rgt1 hyper‑phosphorylation and release from the HXK2 promoter, linking extracellular glucose signals to transcriptional regulation of HXK2. {PubMed:16528100}. PKA3 (encoded by the TPK3 gene) is one of the three catalytic subunits of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase A (PKA) complex in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. In the context of the study, Tpk3 functions as a negative regulator of the TPK1 promoter: it inhibits promoter activity and helps maintain a repressive chromatin conformation under non‑stress conditions. During heat shock, the presence of Tpk3 (together with Tpk2) prevents the up‑regulation of TPK1, indicating that Tpk3 contributes to the autoregulatory feedback loop that fine‑tunes PKA signaling by opposing the chromatin remodeling required for TPK1 activation. The article also notes that Tpk3 can localize to processing bodies (PBs) during glucose starvation and hyper‑osmotic stress, suggesting a role in stress‑specific subcellular compartmentalization of PKA activity. {PubMed:32599085}. The article describes PKA3 as the yeast gene TPK3, one of the three catalytic subunits of protein kinase A (PKA).  Tpk3 participates in the cellular response to heat stress by modulating translation and the formation of messenger‑RNA granules.  Under mild heat stress (37 °C, 30 min) Tpk3 aggregates into cytoplasmic foci that depend on translation inhibition; these foci are distinct from canonical stress granules (SGs) or processing bodies (PBs).  Under severe heat stress (46 °C, 10 min) Tpk3 relocates to SGs/PBs together with Tpk2 and other translation initiation factors (eIF4G, eIF4E, Pab1).  Deletion of TPK3 reduces the number of SGs/PBs formed during heat stress, diminishes the translational arrest normally observed, and alters the polysome profile, indicating that Tpk3 is required for proper translational repression in response to heat shock.  Biochemically, Tpk3 is enriched in granule fractions after severe stress, and its kinase activity is not altered by heat stress nor required for its aggregation into granules.  Overall, Tpk3 functions as a catalytic subunit of PKA that promotes translational inhibition and contributes to the assembly of stress‑induced mRNA granules during heat stress. {PubMed:29045428}. PKA3 (encoded by the TPK3 gene) is one of three catalytic subunits of the yeast cAMP‑dependent protein kinase (cAPK, also called protein kinase A). It can phosphorylate typical cAPK substrates—including the regulatory R subunit, the glycolytic regulator FruP₂ase, and other standard peptide substrates—when present at sufficient levels. In wild‑type cells TPK3 is expressed at very low levels, resulting in barely detectable cAPK activity both in vitro and in vivo. Overexpression of TPK3 alone modestly raises activity, but high catalytic activity is achieved only when the regulatory subunit gene BCY1 is co‑overexpressed, indicating that excess regulatory subunit is required for efficient holo‑enzyme formation and activity. Thus, the primary function of PKA3 is to serve as a catalytic component of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase complex, with its physiological impact limited by its normally low transcriptional expression. {PubMed:8386630}. PKA3 (also called TPK3) encodes one of the three catalytic subunits of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase (PKA) in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.  In the context of this study, Tpk3 participates in the glucose‑ and Ras‑induced inhibition of the anaphase‑promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C).  Although Tpk1, Tpk2 and Tpk3 have overlapping (redundant) roles in transmitting the glucose signal to APC/C, Tpk3 is less efficient than Tpk2 at normal expression levels, likely because it is expressed at lower levels and has lower catalytic activity.  When overexpressed, Tpk3 can inhibit APC/C as effectively as Tpk2, indicating that its catalytic activity is sufficient for this function.  Thus, PKA3 functions as a catalytic component of the PKA signaling pathway that negatively regulates APC/C activity during mitosis in response to elevated cAMP levels triggered by glucose or activated Ras proteins. {PubMed:12724382}. PKA3 (also known as TPK3) encodes one of the three catalytic subunits of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase (cAPK) in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The cAPK complex consists of a regulatory subunit (BCY1) that binds cAMP and up to three catalytic subunits (TPK1, TPK2, TPK3). Although deletion of all three catalytic subunits is lethal, cells can grow with any single subunit, indicating functional redundancy. The article demonstrates that the catalytic subunits, including PKA3/TPK3, are required for the full expression of stress‑induced thermotolerance: sublethal heat induces thermotolerance partially via these subunits, whereas induction of thermotolerance by the cytokinin 2iP or ethanol is completely dependent on them. Additionally, the catalytic subunits influence trehalose metabolism during heat stress, suggesting a role in the phosphorylation‑based regulation of enzymes involved in trehalose synthesis and degradation. {PubMed:1336794}. PKA3 (encoded by TPK3) encodes a catalytic subunit of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase A (PKA) that plays multiple roles in the regulation of mRNA metabolism and translation in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. In exponentially growing cells, Tpk3 associates with translation initiation components such as the poly(A)‑binding protein Pab1 and the small‑ribosomal subunit protein Rps3, indicating a direct interaction with the 48S pre‑initiation complex. Upon glucose starvation, this interaction is lost and Tpk3 relocalises to cytoplasmic mRNA‑silencing granules, first accumulating in processing bodies (PBs) and later also in stress granules (SGs). Kinase activity of Tpk3 is required for its proper recruitment to pre‑formed PBs. Deletion of TPK3 disrupts normal granule dynamics: granules form even in the presence of glucose, they contain atypical protein compositions (including the translation factors Rpg1 and Rps3), and they fail to efficiently sequester mRNAs such as ENO2. Consequently, tpk3Δ cells exhibit an uncoupling of translational inhibition from granule formation during glucose starvation, a modest increase in basal translation, and a faster translational recovery when glucose is re‑added. Moreover, loss of TPK3 leads to elevated protein levels of the cap‑binding scaffold eIF4G1 and the eIF3 subunit Rpg1 during stationary phase, suggesting that PKA3 normally limits the abundance of these initiation factors post‑transcriptionally. Overall, PKA3 functions as a key regulator that links nutrient signalling to multiple stages of mRNA fate—interacting with the translation machinery, controlling the assembly and composition of PBs/SGs, and modulating translation initiation and recovery under nutrient stress. {PubMed:22899713}. PKA3 encodes the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase catalytic subunit in Saccharomyces yeasts. When placed under the control of inducible promoters (CHA1 or MET25), its overexpression reaches toxic levels, making it useful as a counter‑selection marker: activation of the promoter leads to cell death, allowing selection for loss of the plasmid or for ‘loop‑out’ events after genomic integration. {PubMed:10923025}.
Curated_Functions: Catalyzes phosphorylation of typical cAMP‑dependent protein kinase substrates, including the regulatory subunit BCY1 and fructose‑1,6‑bisphosphatase, as a catalytic component of the PKA holoenzyme. {PubMed:8386630}. Mediates hyper‑phosphorylation of the transcription factor Rgt1 in response to high glucose, causing its release from the HXK2 promoter and enabling HXK2 transcription. {PubMed:16528100}. Represses the TPK1 promoter, maintaining a repressive chromatin state and preventing heat‑shock‑induced up‑regulation of TPK1 as part of an autoregulatory feedback loop. {PubMed:32599085}. Contributes to glucose‑and Ras‑dependent inhibition of the anaphase‑promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C), acting redundantly with Tpk1 and Tpk2; overexpression enhances APC/C inhibition. {PubMed:12724382}. Supports normal SUC2 (invertase) expression and participates in PKA‑mediated regulation of invertase levels, particularly during growth on lactate with low glucose. {PubMed:25810078}. Promotes translational repression and the assembly of stress granules and processing bodies during heat stress, being required for proper SG/PB formation and translational arrest of specific mRNAs. {PubMed:29045428, PubMed:22899713}. Associates with translation initiation factors and the 48S pre‑initiation complex; upon glucose starvation relocalises to processing bodies and stress granules, where its kinase activity is required for recruitment, and its loss alters granule composition, increases basal translation, accelerates translational recovery, and elevates eIF4G1 and eIF3 subunit Rpg1 levels. {PubMed:22899713, PubMed:32599085}. Is required for full expression of stress‑induced thermotolerance and contributes to trehalose accumulation during sublethal heat stress, independently of intracellular cAMP changes. {PubMed:1336794}.

Merged_Functions: TPK1 encodes one of the three catalytic subunits of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase A (PKA) complex in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.  The Tpk1 catalytic subunit participates in the PKA signaling circuit that controls cellular responses to environmental changes.  Under heat shock and osmotic stress the TPK1 gene is transcriptionally up‑regulated, a process that requires the transcription factors Msn2/4, Sok2 and Gis1.  Activation of the TPK1 promoter is accompanied by eviction of three positioned nucleosomes (N‑2, N‑1 and N+1) through the coordinated action of ATP‑dependent chromatin‑remodeling complexes SWI/SNF, INO80 and RSC (with ISW1 also contributing).  Recruitment of SWI/SNF to the promoter is Msn2/4‑dependent, and the catalytic activity of Tpk1 itself is necessary for the nucleosome rearrangement that permits promoter opening.  Tpk1 also binds its own promoter during early heat‑shock, whereas Tpk2 binds later and acts to re‑establish a repressive chromatin state, illustrating an autoregulatory feedback loop.  Thus, TPK1 functions both as a catalytic enzyme that phosphorylates downstream targets in the PKA pathway and as a regulator of its own transcription through stress‑induced chromatin remodeling. {PubMed:32599085}. Encodes one of the three catalytic subunits (Tpk1) of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase (PKA) in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Tpk1 participates in the glucose‑ and Ras‑induced activation of PKA, which acts as a negative regulator of the anaphase‑promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C). Genetic experiments show that loss of TPK1 alone does not abolish APC/C inhibition, indicating that Tpk1 functions redundantly with the other PKA catalytic subunits Tpk2 and Tpk3. Overexpression of TPK1 only marginally decreases the viability of APC mutant strains, suggesting that Tpk1 is capable of mediating APC/C inhibition but is less efficient than Tpk2 or Tpk3. {PubMed:12724382}. TPK1 encodes one of the three catalytic subunits (Tpk1p, Tpk2p, Tpk3p) of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase (cAPK) in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.  The enzyme complex mediates nutrient‑sensing and growth regulation via the Ras/cAMP signaling cascade.  Tpk1p phosphorylates downstream targets, notably the neutral trehalase Nth1p, and this phosphorylation is required for maintaining neutral trehalase activity during heat stress.  The study shows that cells retaining only TPK1 (or TPK2) can sustain neutral trehalase activity, whereas cells lacking both TPK1 and TPK2 (tpk1tpk2TPK3) exhibit a severe loss of neutral trehalase activity under heat shock, which can be rescued by re‑introducing TPK1.  TPK1 is functionally redundant with TPK2 and TPK3, but the catalytic subunits display a hierarchy of activity (Tpk2 > Tpk1 > Tpk3).  Additionally, TPK1 can complement the loss of the other TPK genes, indicating overlapping physiological roles. {PubMed:9738892}. TPK1 encodes one of the three catalytic subunits (Tpk1, Tpk2, Tpk3) of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase (PKA) in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.  It interacts with the regulatory subunit Bcy1 and becomes active upon binding cAMP.  In the context of this study, Tpk1 (along with Tpk2 and Tpk3) contributes to the regulation of the SUC2 gene: PKA activity mediated by the Tpk isoenzymes decreases invertase (SUC2 product) levels when cells grow without glucose and enhances invertase expression when cells are exposed to low glucose.  Strains expressing only Tpk1 show reduced, but still detectable, induction of invertase compared with wild‑type, indicating that Tpk1 participates in the glucose‑responsive control of SUC2 transcription, although the effect is not isoform‑specific. {PubMed:25810078}. TPK1 encodes the catalytic subunit (Tpk1p) of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase A (PKA) in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.  The enzyme participates in the glucose‑dependent signalling cascade that raises intracellular cAMP, leading to activation of PKA.  Activated PKA stimulates glycolysis, promotes rapid cell‑cycle progression, mobilises trehalose and glycogen, represses stress‑related and gluconeogenic genes and induces growth‑related genes.  Tpk1p itself becomes phosphorylated in response to glucose addition; this phosphorylation increases its catalytic efficiency toward the peptide substrate kemptide.  The phosphorylation state of Tpk1p shifts toward more highly phosphorylated isoforms during the transition from respiratory to fermentative metabolism (high glucose) and reverts to less phosphorylated forms during the diauxic shift or stationary phase.  These changes depend on the GPCR‑mediated cAMP signal and represent a fine‑tuning mechanism for PKA activity in response to environmental carbon sources. {PubMed:16226873}. TPK1 encodes one of the catalytic subunits of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase (cAPK) in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The study shows that Tpk1, together with Tpk2, mediates the glucose‑induced signaling that leads to phosphorylation of isocitrate lyase (Icl). This phosphorylation is required for the rapid, reversible (short‑term) inactivation of Icl after glucose addition, and Tpk1 also participates in the signaling cascade that ultimately results in the slower, irreversible (long‑term) proteolytic degradation of Icl. Although none of the three TPK genes is essential on its own, at least one catalytic subunit must be present for cell viability, and strains possessing only TPK1 retain the normal pattern of Icl inactivation observed in wild‑type cells. {PubMed:8641464}. TPK1 encodes a two‑pore (tandem‑pore) potassium channel that is localized to the vacuolar (tonoplast) membrane. When expressed in yeast vacuoles, the TPK1 protein forms an ion channel that is activated by micromolar concentrations of cytosolic Ca²⁺, displays no voltage dependence over a range of ±80 mV, and conducts K⁺ with strong selectivity over Na⁺ (the channel contains the conserved GYG motif in both pore loops). The channel shows an asymmetric single‑channel conductance of about 75 pS for inward currents and 40 pS for outward currents in symmetric 100 mM KCl. Thus, TPK1 functions as a voltage‑independent, Ca²⁺‑activated, K⁺‑selective vacuolar ion channel, distinct from the non‑selective slow‑vacuolar (SV) channel, and likely contributes to vacuolar K⁺ homeostasis. {PubMed:16113216}. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, TPK1 encodes the catalytic subunit Tpk1p of protein kinase A. While the three Tpk isoforms are functionally redundant for cell viability, each regulates distinct cellular processes. Tpk1p is specifically required for amino‑acid biosynthesis and, together with Tpk2p and Tpk3p, participates in the regulation of filamentous (hyphal) growth. {PubMed:27678009}. The article notes that, unlike the fission‑yeast Pka1 catalytic subunit, mutations in the Tpk1‑containing PKA holoenzyme have not been found to extend lifespan in budding yeast. {PubMed:16822282}. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, TPK1 encodes one of the three catalytic subunits of protein kinase A (PKA).  Microarray analyses of tpk1 mutant strains showed that Tpk1 influences transcriptional regulation, specifically affecting the expression of genes required for branched‑chain amino acid biosynthesis. {PubMed:17367210}. PKA1 encodes one of the catalytic subunits (Tpk1p) of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase (cAPK) in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The enzyme phosphorylates downstream targets such as the neutral trehalase Nth1p, and a basal level of this phosphorylation is required to keep neutral trehalase active and stable during heat stress. Loss of PKA1 activity (as in tpk1tpk2TPK3 mutants) leads to a strong reduction of cAPK activity, rapid heat‑induced inactivation of neutral trehalase, accumulation of trehalose, and decreased thermotolerance. Restoration of PKA1 expression rescues the heat‑stress phenotype, indicating that PKA1‑mediated phosphorylation is essential for maintenance of neutral trehalase activity and for proper heat‑shock recovery. PKA1 encodes the catalytic subunit (Tpk1p) of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase A (PKA) in *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*.  The enzyme phosphorylates downstream targets to control a wide range of cellular processes, including stimulation of glycolysis, rapid progression through the cell cycle, mobilization of trehalose and glycogen, repression of stress‑related and gluconeogenic genes, and induction of growth‑related genes.  Its activity is regulated by intracellular cAMP levels generated via a glucose‑sensing GPCR pathway, by association with the regulatory subunit Bcy1p, and by reversible autophosphorylation of Tpk1p itself, which increases the catalytic efficiency toward substrates such as kemptide.  Phosphorylation of Tpk1p rises during the transition from respiratory to fermentative metabolism (high glucose) and declines during stationary or respiratory phases, providing a fine‑tuning mechanism for PKA activity in response to nutrient conditions. {PubMed:16226873}. PKA1 encodes the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase catalytic subunit, the central regulator of the PKA signaling cascade in Schizosaccharomyces japonicus. Deletion of the single pka1 gene alters the expression of at least 373 downstream genes, including kinases, phosphatases and transcriptional regulators. Through this broad regulatory network Pka1p controls multiple cellular processes: it promotes normal cell length, positively influences hyphal elongation (its loss shortens the mycelial zone), regulates dimorphic switching, modulates aging and chronological survival, affects sporulation efficiency, and is required for proper stress responses (oxidative stress, pH extremes, temperature shifts, and certain osmotic or chemical stresses). Transcriptomic analysis further links Pka1p to metabolic pathways such as carbohydrate metabolism and transport, protein translation and modification, mitochondrial organization, ribosome biogenesis, and oxidative‑stress defense. The authors conclude that the single S. japonicus pka1 gene fulfills the combined functions of the multiple TPK catalytic subunits found in budding yeasts. {PubMed:27678009}. According to the article, Pka1 regulates glycogen synthesis (glycogenesis), glucose repression, the transition from mitosis to meiosis, chronological aging, and stress responses to high KCl and CaCl₂. Encodes one of the two catalytic subunits of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase A (PKA) in Ashbya gossypii. TPK2 encodes one of the three catalytic subunits of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase A (PKA) in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Thus, Tpk2 functions both as a catalytic subunit of PKA and as an autoregulatory factor that limits TPK1 transcription by modulating promoter chromatin structure. {PubMed:32599085}. TPK2 encodes one of three redundant catalytic subunits of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase (cAPK) in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The catalytic subunits are released from the regulatory BCY1 subunit upon cAMP binding and mediate phosphorylation of downstream targets in the Ras/cAMP signaling cascade, which controls nutrient sensing and growth regulation. TPK2 can complement the other TPK genes (TPK1 and TPK3) and displays a higher intrinsic activity, establishing a functional hierarchy of Tpk2 > Tpk1 > Tpk3. Phosphorylation by Tpk2 (together with Tpk1) is required for the maintenance of neutral trehalase (Nth1p) activity and stability during heat stress, indicating its role in stress‑responsive regulation of this enzyme. {PubMed:9738892}. TPK2 encodes one of the three catalytic subunits (Tpk1, Tpk2, Tpk3) of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase A (PKA) in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. In the regulation of the SUC2 gene, which encodes invertase, Tpk2 contributes to the low‑glucose‑induced activation of SUC2: strains that retain only Tpk2 reach only about half of the maximal invertase activity observed in wild‑type cells under low‑glucose conditions. Although Tpk2 is not essential for SUC2 induction, its activity, together with the other Tpk isoforms, modulates both repression (in the absence of glucose) and activation (in the presence of low glucose) of invertase expression. {PubMed:25810078}. TPK2 encodes one of the catalytic subunits of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase (PKA) in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. FUNCTION: Component of the transcription coactivator SAGA complex. SAGA acts as a general cofactor required for essentially all RNA polymerase II transcription (PubMed:10864329, PubMed:25216679, PubMed:28918903). At the promoters, SAGA is required for transcription pre-initiation complex (PIC) recruitment. It influences RNA polymerase II transcriptional activity through different activities such as TBP interaction (via core/TAF module) and promoter selectivity, interaction with transcription activators (via Tra1/SPT module), and chromatin modification through histone acetylation (via HAT module) and deubiquitination (via DUB module) (PubMed:10580001, PubMed:31969703). SAGA preferentially acetylates histones H3 (to form H3K9ac, H3K14ac, H3K18ac and H3K23ac) and H2B and deubiquitinates histone H2B (PubMed:10026213). SAGA interacts with DNA via upstream activating sequences (UASs) (PubMed:11485989). Also identified in a modified version of SAGA named SALSA or SLIK (PubMed:12186975, PubMed:12446794). The cleavage of SPT7 and the absence of the SPT8 subunit in SLIK neither drive any major conformational differences in its structure compared with SAGA, nor significantly affect HAT, DUB, or DNA-binding activities (PubMed:33864814). SPT3 is required for recruitment of TATA-binding protein (TBP) to SAGA-dependent promoters (PubMed:12370284). During SAGA-mediated transcriptional inhibition, SPT3 and SPT8 prevent binding of TBP to the TATA box (PubMed:10611242). Required for diploid filamentous growth and haploid invasive growth (PubMed:12072450). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10026213, ECO:0000269|PubMed:10580001, ECO:0000269|PubMed:10611242, ECO:0000269|PubMed:10864329, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11485989, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12072450, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12186975, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12370284, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12446794, ECO:0000269|PubMed:25216679, ECO:0000269|PubMed:28918903, ECO:0000269|PubMed:31969703, ECO:0000269|PubMed:33864814}.

FUNCTION: Component of the ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase, a multisubunit transmembrane complex that is part of the mitochondrial electron transport chain which drives oxidative phosphorylation. The respiratory chain contains 3 multisubunit complexes succinate dehydrogenase (complex II, CII), ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase (cytochrome b-c1 complex, complex III, CIII) and cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV, CIV), that cooperate to transfer electrons derived from NADH and succinate to molecular oxygen, creating an electrochemical gradient over the inner membrane that drives transmembrane transport and the ATP synthase. The cytochrome b-c1 complex catalyzes electron transfer from ubiquinol to cytochrome c, linking this redox reaction to translocation of protons across the mitochondrial inner membrane, with protons being carried across the membrane as hydrogens on the quinol. In the process called Q cycle, 2 protons are consumed from the matrix, 4 protons are released into the intermembrane space and 2 electrons are passed to cytochrome c (Probable). Cytochrome c1 is a catalytic core subunit containing a c-type heme. It transfers electrons from the [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster of the Rieske protein to cytochrome c (PubMed:18390544). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:18390544, ECO:0000305|PubMed:11880631}.

It can also use Ins(1,3,4,5,6)P5 as a substrate and act as a diphosphoinositol polyphosphate synthase to generate two different isomers of PP-InsP4 (PubMed:11311242). Inositol polyphosphates may be involved in the regulation of chromatin remodeling of transcription (PubMed:12434012). Regulates nuclear mRNA export via inositol phosphate metabolism (PubMed:10390371, PubMed:10683435). Also has lipid kinase activity, transforming the lipid inositol phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2) into phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate (PI(3,4,5)P3) in the nucleus (PubMed:16123124). Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Mitochondrial membrane ATP synthase (F(1)F(0) ATP synthase or Complex V) produces ATP from ADP in the presence of a proton gradient across the membrane which is generated by electron transport complexes of the respiratory chain. F-type ATPases consist of two structural domains, F(1) - containing the extramembraneous catalytic core, and F(0) - containing the membrane proton channel, linked together by a central stalk and a peripheral stalk. During catalysis, ATP synthesis in the catalytic domain of F(1) is coupled via a rotary mechanism of the central stalk subunits to proton translocation. Subunits alpha and beta form the catalytic core in F(1). Rotation of the central stalk against the surrounding alpha(3)beta(3) subunits leads to hydrolysis of ATP in three separate catalytic sites on the beta subunits. Subunit alpha does not bear the catalytic high-affinity ATP-binding sites (By similarity). {ECO:0000250}.

FUNCTION: Component of the cytochrome c oxidase, the last enzyme in the mitochondrial electron transport chain which drives oxidative phosphorylation. The respiratory chain contains 3 multisubunit complexes succinate dehydrogenase (complex II, CII), ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase (cytochrome b-c1 complex, complex III, CIII) and cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV, CIV), that cooperate to transfer electrons derived from NADH and succinate to molecular oxygen, creating an electrochemical gradient over the inner membrane that drives transmembrane transport and the ATP synthase. Cytochrome c oxidase is the component of the respiratory chain that catalyzes the reduction of oxygen to water. Electrons originating from reduced cytochrome c in the intermembrane space (IMS) are transferred via the dinuclear copper A center (CU(A)) of COX2 and heme A of COX1 to the active site in COX1, a binuclear center (BNC) formed by heme A3 and copper B (CU(B)). The BNC reduces molecular oxygen to 2 water molecules using 4 electrons from cytochrome c in the IMS and 4 protons from the mitochondrial matrix. {ECO:0000305|PubMed:30598554}.

FUNCTION: Component of the ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase, a multisubunit transmembrane complex that is part of the mitochondrial electron transport chain which drives oxidative phosphorylation. The respiratory chain contains 3 multisubunit complexes succinate dehydrogenase (complex II, CII), ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase (cytochrome b-c1 complex, complex III, CIII) and cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV, CIV), that cooperate to transfer electrons derived from NADH and succinate to molecular oxygen, creating an electrochemical gradient over the inner membrane that drives transmembrane transport and the ATP synthase. The cytochrome b-c1 complex catalyzes electron transfer from ubiquinol to cytochrome c, linking this redox reaction to translocation of protons across the mitochondrial inner membrane, with protons being carried across the membrane as hydrogens on the quinol. In the process called Q cycle, 2 protons are consumed from the matrix, 4 protons are released into the intermembrane space and 2 electrons are passed to cytochrome c. {ECO:0000305|PubMed:11880631}.

FUNCTION: Mevalonate kinase; part of the second module of ergosterol biosynthesis pathway that includes the middle steps of the pathway (PubMed:1645230). ERG12 converts mevalonate into 5-phosphomevalonate (PubMed:1645230). The second module is carried out in the vacuole and involves the formation of farnesyl diphosphate, which is also an important intermediate in the biosynthesis of ubiquinone, dolichol, heme and prenylated proteins. Activity by the mevalonate kinase ERG12 first converts mevalonate into 5-phosphomevalonate. 5-phosphomevalonate is then further converted to 5-diphosphomevalonate by the phosphomevalonate kinase ERG8. Finally the farnesyl diphosphate synthase ERG20 catalyzes the sequential condensation of isopentenyl pyrophosphate with dimethylallyl pyrophosphate, and then with the resultant geranylpyrophosphate to the ultimate product farnesyl pyrophosphate (PubMed:32679672). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:1645230, ECO:0000303|PubMed:32679672}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Component of the ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase, a multisubunit transmembrane complex that is part of the mitochondrial electron transport chain which drives oxidative phosphorylation. The respiratory chain contains 3 multisubunit complexes succinate dehydrogenase (complex II, CII), ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase (cytochrome b-c1 complex, complex III, CIII) and cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV, CIV), that cooperate to transfer electrons derived from NADH and succinate to molecular oxygen, creating an electrochemical gradient over the inner membrane that drives transmembrane transport and the ATP synthase. The cytochrome b-c1 complex catalyzes electron transfer from ubiquinol to cytochrome c, linking this redox reaction to translocation of protons across the mitochondrial inner membrane, with protons being carried across the membrane as hydrogens on the quinol. In the process called Q cycle, 2 protons are consumed from the matrix, 4 protons are released into the intermembrane space and 2 electrons are passed to cytochrome c (Probable). The Rieske protein is a catalytic core subunit containing a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster (PubMed:18390544). It cycles between 2 conformational states during catalysis to transfer electrons from the quinol bound in the Q(0) site in cytochrome b (COB) to cytochrome c1 (CYT1) (Probable) (PubMed:1657998, PubMed:2538628). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:1657998, ECO:0000269|PubMed:18390544, ECO:0000269|PubMed:2538628, ECO:0000305|PubMed:11880631, ECO:0000305|PubMed:30598556}.

FUNCTION: DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates. Second largest component of RNA polymerases II which synthesizes mRNA precursors and many functional non-coding RNAs. Proposed to contribute to the polymerase catalytic activity and forms the polymerase active center together with the largest subunit. Pol II is the central component of the basal RNA polymerase II transcription machinery. During a transcription cycle, Pol II, general transcription factors and the Mediator complex assemble as the preinitiation complex (PIC) at the promoter. 11-15 base pairs of DNA surrounding the transcription start site are melted and the single-stranded DNA template strand of the promoter is positioned deeply within the central active site cleft of Pol II to form the open complex. After synthesis of about 30 bases of RNA, Pol II releases its contacts with the core promoter and the rest of the transcription machinery (promoter clearance) and enters the stage of transcription elongation in which it moves on the template as the transcript elongates. Pol II appears to oscillate between inactive and active conformations at each step of nucleotide addition. Pol II is composed of mobile elements that move relative to each other. The core element with the central large cleft comprises RPB3, RBP10, RPB11, RPB12 and regions of RPB1 and RPB2 forming the active center. The clamp element (portions of RPB1, RPB2 and RPB3) is connected to the core through a set of flexible switches and moves to open and close the cleft. The cleft is surrounded by jaws: an upper jaw formed by portions of RBP1, RPB2 and RPB9, and a lower jaw. The jaws are thought to grab the incoming DNA template. The fork loop 1 (RPB2) interacts with the RNA-DNA hybrid, possibly stabilizing it.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase; part of the second module of ergosterol biosynthesis pathway that includes the middle steps of the pathway (PubMed:8096487). ERG20 catalyzes the sequential condensation of isopentenyl pyrophosphate with dimethylallyl pyrophosphate, and then with the resultant geranylpyrophosphate to the ultimate product farnesyl pyrophosphate (PubMed:8096487). The second module is carried out in the vacuole and involves the formation of farnesyl diphosphate, which is also an important intermediate in the biosynthesis of ubiquinone, dolichol, heme and prenylated proteins. Activity by the mevalonate kinase ERG12 first converts mevalonate into 5-phosphomevalonate. 5-phosphomevalonate is then further converted to 5-diphosphomevalonate by the phosphomevalonate kinase ERG8. The diphosphomevalonate decarboxylase MVD1/ERG19 then produces isopentenyl diphosphate. The isopentenyl-diphosphate delta-isomerase IDI1 then catalyzes the 1,3-allylic rearrangement of the homoallylic substrate isopentenyl (IPP) to its highly electrophilic allylic isomer, dimethylallyl diphosphate (DMAPP). Finally the farnesyl diphosphate synthase ERG20 catalyzes the sequential condensation of isopentenyl pyrophosphate with dimethylallyl pyrophosphate, and then with the resultant geranylpyrophosphate to the ultimate product farnesyl pyrophosphate (PubMed:32679672). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:8096487, ECO:0000303|PubMed:32679672}.

In the process called Q cycle, 2 protons are consumed from the matrix, 4 protons are released into the intermembrane space and 2 electrons are passed to cytochrome c. {ECO:0000305|PubMed:11880631}.

The FBP1 gene encodes the yeast fructose bisphosphatase enzyme, which catalyzes the key gluconeogenic reaction that hydrolyzes fructose‑1,6‑bisphosphate to fructose‑6‑phosphate and inorganic phosphate. The enzyme functions as a tetramer of identical ~41–42 kDa subunits and is inhibited by metabolic effectors such as fructose‑2,6‑bisphosphate and AMP. FBP1 is present as a single copy in the haploid S. cerevisiae genome; its transcription produces an ~1350‑nt mRNA that is detectable only under derepressed (glucose‑exhausted) conditions, indicating regulation by catabolite repression. Loss of FBP1 activity (null mutation) results in a hexose auxotrophic phenotype on gluconeogenic carbon sources, confirming its essential role in gluconeogenesis. In addition to transcriptional control, the enzyme is subject to catabolite inactivation via glucose‑induced phosphorylation and subsequent proteolysis. {PubMed:3003364}. FBP1 encodes the yeast fructose‑1,6‑bisphosphatase enzyme, which catalyzes the dephosphorylation of fructose‑1,6‑bisphosphate to fructose‑6‑phosphate, a key step of gluconeogenesis. The enzyme is required for growth on non‑fermentable carbon sources such as ethanol; fbp1::HIS3 null mutants cannot grow on ethanol and lack FBPase activity. Its expression is tightly regulated: transcription is repressed by glucose, the enzyme is inhibited by AMP and fructose‑2,6‑bisphosphate, undergoes rapid reversible inactivation after glucose addition, and is subject to irreversible degradation several minutes after glucose addition. {PubMed:2841162}. FBP1 encodes the fructose‑1,6‑bisphosphatase that catalyzes the key step of gluconeogenesis.  In Saccharomyces cerevisiae its expression is normally repressed by glucose but is strongly induced by DNA‑damage caused by low doses of methyl methanesulfonate (MMS) even in glucose‑rich medium.  The protein influences several cellular processes beyond its metabolic role:
• Deletion of FBP1 reduces sensitivity to MMS, whereas over‑expression increases MMS sensitivity, shortens chronological life span, and enhances induction of the DNA‑damage‑responsive RNR2 promoter after MMS treatment. 
• Cells lacking FBP1 produce markedly less reactive oxygen species (ROS) after MMS exposure and during early stages of chronological aging, leading to higher survival and the ability to form colonies after prolonged MMS treatment. 
• Over‑production of FBP1 raises ROS levels after MMS and accelerates loss of viability during aging. 
• FBP1 is required for growth on non‑fermentable carbon sources (ethanol/glycerol), reflecting its essential function in gluconeogenesis. 
Thus, FBP1 functions as the central gluconeogenic enzyme and also modulates the cellular response to DNA damage, oxidative stress, and aging, likely through regulation of ROS production rather than direct effects on DNA repair. {PubMed:16199065}. The fbp1 gene of Schizosaccharomyces pombe encodes the enzyme fructose‑1,6‑bisphosphatase.  This enzyme is a key component of the gluconeogenic pathway, converting fructose‑1,6‑bisphosphate to fructose‑6‑phosphate.  Transcription of fbp1 is tightly regulated by nutrient signals: it is repressed by glucose through activation of the cAMP‑dependent protein kinase A (PKA) pathway and derepressed during glucose starvation via a stress‑activated mitogen‑activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascade.  Thus, fbp1 functions both as a metabolic enzyme and as a model gene for studying glucose‑responsive transcriptional control. {PubMed:11238405}. Encodes fructose‑1,6‑bisphosphatase, a key enzyme of the gluconeogenic pathway in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The enzyme participates in the conversion of metabolites during gluconeogenesis and its expression is subject to glucose repression, being derepressed under non‑fermentable carbon sources in a Cat8p‑dependent manner, co‑regulated with other gluconeogenic genes such as PCK1, ICL1 and MLS1. {PubMed:9894915}. FBP1 encodes the enzyme fructose‑1,6‑bisphosphatase in Schizosaccharomyces pombe. Its transcription is strongly repressed by glucose, a regulation that depends on a glucose‑triggered cyclic AMP (cAMP) signaling cascade which activates protein kinase A to inhibit fbp1 expression. Under glucose starvation, fbp1 transcription is activated via the Spc1p stress‑activated MAP kinase pathway and the Atf1p‑Pcr1p bZIP transcription factor complex, which act through upstream activating sequences (UAS1 and UAS2). Thus, FBP1 functions as a key gluconeogenic enzyme whose expression is tightly controlled by nutrient‑responsive signaling pathways. {PubMed:12456004}.
