FUNCTION: Component of the ribosome, a large ribonucleoprotein complex responsible for the synthesis of proteins in the cell. The small ribosomal subunit (SSU) binds messenger RNAs (mRNAs) and translates the encoded message by selecting cognate aminoacyl-transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules. The large subunit (LSU) contains the ribosomal catalytic site termed the peptidyl transferase center (PTC), which catalyzes the formation of peptide bonds, thereby polymerizing the amino acids delivered by tRNAs into a polypeptide chain. The nascent polypeptides leave the ribosome through a tunnel in the LSU and interact with protein factors that function in enzymatic processing, targeting, and the membrane insertion of nascent chains at the exit of the ribosomal tunnel. {ECO:0000305|PubMed:22096102}.

FUNCTION: Regulation of oxygen dependent gene expression. It modulates the expression of Iso-1 (CYP1) and Iso-2 (CYP3) cytochrome c. FUNCTION: Ubiquitin exists either covalently attached to another protein, or free (unanchored). When covalently bound, it is conjugated to target proteins via an isopeptide bond either as a monomer (monoubiquitin), a polymer linked via different Lys residues of the ubiquitin (polyubiquitin chains) or a linear polymer linked via the initiator Met of the ubiquitin (linear polyubiquitin chains). Polyubiquitin chains, when attached to a target protein, have different functions depending on the Lys residue of the ubiquitin that is linked: Lys-6-linked may be involved in DNA repair; Lys-11-linked is involved in ERAD (endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation) and in cell-cycle regulation; Lys-29-linked is involved in lysosomal degradation; Lys-33-linked is involved in kinase modification; Lys-48-linked is involved in protein degradation via the proteasome; Lys-63-linked is involved in endocytosis, and DNA-damage responses. Linear polymer chains formed via attachment by the initiator Met lead to cell signaling. Ubiquitin is usually conjugated to Lys residues of target proteins, however, in rare cases, conjugation to Cys or Ser residues has been observed. When polyubiquitin is free (unanchored-polyubiquitin), it also has distinct roles, such as in activation of protein kinases, and in signaling (By similarity). {ECO:0000250|UniProtKB:P0CG47}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Component of the cytochrome c oxidase, the last enzyme in the mitochondrial electron transport chain which drives oxidative phosphorylation. The respiratory chain contains 3 multisubunit complexes succinate dehydrogenase (complex II, CII), ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase (cytochrome b-c1 complex, complex III, CIII) and cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV, CIV), that cooperate to transfer electrons derived from NADH and succinate to molecular oxygen, creating an electrochemical gradient over the inner membrane that drives transmembrane transport and the ATP synthase. Cytochrome c oxidase is the component of the respiratory chain that catalyzes the reduction of oxygen to water. Electrons originating from reduced cytochrome c in the intermembrane space (IMS) are transferred via the dinuclear copper A center (CU(A)) of COX2 and heme A of COX1 to the active site in COX1, a binuclear center (BNC) formed by heme A3 and copper B (CU(B)). The BNC reduces molecular oxygen to 2 water molecules using 4 electrons from cytochrome c in the IMS and 4 protons from the mitochondrial matrix. {ECO:0000305|PubMed:30598554}.

FUNCTION: Releases the supercoiling and torsional tension of DNA introduced during the DNA replication and transcription by transiently cleaving and rejoining one strand of the DNA duplex. The scissile phosphodiester is attacked by the catalytic tyrosine of the enzyme, resulting in the formation of a DNA-(5'-phosphotyrosyl)-enzyme intermediate and the expulsion of a 3'-OH DNA strand. FUNCTION: Component of the anaphase promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C), a cell cycle-regulated E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase complex that controls progression through mitosis and the G1 phase of the cell cycle. In early mitosis, the APC/C is activated by CDC20 and targets securin PDS1, the B-type cyclin CLB5, and other anaphase inhibitory proteins for proteolysis, thereby triggering the separation of sister chromatids at the metaphase-to-anaphase transition. Merged_Functions: GCD5 encodes the yeast cytoplasmic lysyl‑tRNA synthetase (LysRS), the enzyme that catalyzes the ATP‑dependent attachment of lysine to its cognate tRNA^Lys, producing charged tRNA required for protein synthesis. The gene is identical to KRS1. In addition to this catalytic role, GCD5 is part of an autoregulatory loop: when LysRS activity is reduced (as in the gcd5‑1 mutant), uncharged tRNA^Lys accumulates, activating the GCN2 protein kinase, which phosphorylates eIF‑2α and derepresses translation of the transcription factor GCN4. Elevated GCN4 then binds upstream of GCD5 and stimulates its transcription, increasing LysRS levels. Thus GCD5 functions both as a lysine‑charging enzyme and as a regulatory target within the general amino‑acid control (GCN) response. {PubMed:1505029}. GCD5 is one of the newly identified GCD genes in Saccharomyces cerevisiae that participates in the general control of amino‑acid biosynthesis. Mutations in GCD5 (gcd5‑1) produce the characteristic dual phenotype of constitutive derepression of amino‑acid biosynthetic enzymes (e.g., TRP3, ARG4) and a slow‑growth phenotype, both of which persist even when external amino acids are supplied. Genetic analysis shows that gcd5‑1 is lethal when combined with mutations in the GCN genes (gcn1‑1, gcn2‑1, gcn3‑1, and gcn4‑101), indicating that GCD5 encodes an essential component of the regulatory pathway. The authors propose two possible roles for GCD5 (and other GCD genes): (1) it may encode an aminoacyl‑tRNA synthetase, with gcd5‑1 representing a leaky, non‑conditional synthetase mutant; or (2) it may be involved directly or indirectly in vacuolar amino‑acid transport, influencing intracellular amino‑acid availability and thereby signaling amino‑acid limitation. While a definitive biochemical function is not established, GCD5 is implicated in mediating the signal that links amino‑acid availability to the GCN‑dependent transcriptional control system. {PubMed:3329041}. Encodes a P‑type ion pump (Ca²⁺‑ATPase) that is highly homologous to the PMR2 family. FUNCTION: Second most abundant of three pyruvate decarboxylases (PDC1, PDC5, PDC6) implicated in the nonoxidative conversion of pyruvate to acetaldehyde and carbon dioxide during alcoholic fermentation. The enzyme is also one of five 2-oxo acid decarboxylases (PDC1, PDC5, PDC6, ARO10, and THI3) able to decarboxylate more complex 2-oxo acids (alpha-keto-acids) than pyruvate, which seem mainly involved in amino acid catabolism. Here the enzyme catalyzes the decarboxylation of amino acids, which, in a first step, have been transaminated to the corresponding 2-oxo acids. In a third step, the resulting aldehydes are reduced to alcohols, collectively referred to as fusel oils or alcohols. Its preferred substrates are the transaminated amino acids derived from threonine (2-oxobutanoate), norvaline (2-oxopentanoate), valine (3-methyl-2-oxobutanoate, also alpha-keto-isovalerate), isoleucine ((3S)-3-methyl-2-oxopentanoate, also alpha-keto-beta-methylvalerate), phenylalanine (phenylpyruvate), and tryptophan (3-(indol-3-yl)pyruvate), whereas transaminated leucine is no substrate. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Component of the anaphase promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C), a cell cycle-regulated E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase complex that controls progression through mitosis and the G1 phase of the cell cycle. The APC/C is thought to confer substrate specificity and, in the presence of ubiquitin-conjugating E2 enzymes, it catalyzes the formation of protein-ubiquitin conjugates that are subsequently degraded by the 26S proteasome. In early mitosis, the APC/C is activated by CDC20 and targets securin PDS1, the B-type cyclin CLB5, and other anaphase inhibitory proteins for proteolysis, thereby triggering the separation of sister chromatids at the metaphase-to-anaphase transition. In late mitosis and in G1, degradation of CLB5 allows activation of the APC/C by CDH1, which is needed to destroy CDC20 and the B-type cyclin CLB2 to allow exit from mitosis and creating the low CDK state necessary for cytokinesis and for reforming prereplicative complexes in G1 prior to another round of replication. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10871279, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12413490, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12609981, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7925276, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8423787}.

FUNCTION: Component of the ribosome, a large ribonucleoprotein complex responsible for the synthesis of proteins in the cell. The small ribosomal subunit (SSU) binds messenger RNAs (mRNAs) and translates the encoded message by selecting cognate aminoacyl-transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules. The large subunit (LSU) contains the ribosomal catalytic site termed the peptidyl transferase center (PTC), which catalyzes the formation of peptide bonds, thereby polymerizing the amino acids delivered by tRNAs into a polypeptide chain. The nascent polypeptides leave the ribosome through a tunnel in the LSU and interact with protein factors that function in enzymatic processing, targeting, and the membrane insertion of nascent chains at the exit of the ribosomal tunnel. {ECO:0000305|PubMed:22096102}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Cyclin-dependent protein kinase (CDK) catalytic subunit that regulates multiple cell cycle and metabolic processes in response to nutrient availability. Associates with different cyclins, that control kinase activity, substrate specificity and subcellular location of the kinase. Regulates metabolic processes when associated with PHO80 cyclin family members (PH080, PCL6, PCL7, PCL8 and PCL10), and cell cycle and morphogenesis processes when associated with PCL1,2 cyclin family members (PCL1, PCL2, CLG1, PCL5 and PCL9) (PubMed:10490639, PubMed:10692159, PubMed:11602261, PubMed:12006994, PubMed:12098764, PubMed:12101234, PubMed:12407105, PubMed:12455686, PubMed:12857883, PubMed:15057567, PubMed:15082539, PubMed:15598647, PubMed:15721288, PubMed:16308562, PubMed:16455487, PubMed:3067079, PubMed:7973730, PubMed:8108735, PubMed:8539622, PubMed:9584169, PubMed:9593297, PubMed:9725902, PubMed:9843683). When associated with PHO80, negatively regulates the expression of phosphate-starvation-responsive genes under phosphate-rich conditions (PubMed:3067079, PubMed:8108735). The PHO80-PHO85 cyclin-CDK holoenzyme phosphorylates and inactivates the transcription factor PHO4 by promoting its export to the cytoplasm (PubMed:8108735). PHO80-PHO85 phosphorylates and inactivates protein kinase RIM15 by retaining it in the cytoplasm, antagonizing RIM15-induced entry into stationary phase (PubMed:16308562). PHO80-PHO85 also phosphorylates and inactivates the calcineurin-responsive transcription factor CRZ1, linking cyclin-CDK activity to calcium signaling (PubMed:16455487). PHO80-PHO85 phosphorylates MMR1 (PubMed:12006994). Together with the cyclins PCL6/PCL7 and PCL8/PCL10, negatively controls glycogen accumulation (PubMed:10490639, PubMed:11602261, PubMed:12407105, PubMed:15721288, PubMed:8539622, PubMed:9584169). When associated with cyclins PCL6 and PCL7, controls glycogen phosphorylase and glycogen synthase activities (PubMed:11602261, PubMed:12407105, PubMed:15721288). PCL6-PHO85 and PCL7-PHO85 phosphorylate and inactivate the phosphatase PP1-2 inhibitor GLC8, causing activation of PP1-2, which then dephosphorylates and activates glycogen phosphorylase (PubMed:12407105). PCL7-PHO85 phosphorylate ALY2 (PubMed:12098764). PCL10-PHO85 phosphorylates and negatively regulates glycogen synthase GSY2 (PubMed:9584169). Association with PCL1 and PCL2 is required for cell cycle progression at start in the absence of the CDC28-dependent G1 cyclins CLN1 and CLN2 (PubMed:7973730, PubMed:7973731). PCL1-PHO85 is involved in phosphorylation of the CDK inhibitor (CKI) SIC1, which is required for its ubiquitination and degradation, releasing repression of b-type cyclins and promoting exit from mitosis (PubMed:9725902). When associated with cyclins PCL1 and PCL2, positively controls degradation of sphingoid long chain base kinase LCB4 via phosphorylation of LCB4, which is required for its ubiquitination and degradation (PubMed:15598647). PCL1-PHO85 also phosphorylates HMS1, NCP1 and NPA3, which may all have a role in mitotic exit (PubMed:15082539). PCL2-PHO85 also phosphorylates RVS167, linking cyclin-CDK activity with organization of the actin cytoskeleton (PubMed:12857883, PubMed:9843683). When associated with PCL5, positively controls degradation of transcription factor GCN4 via phosphorylation of GCN4, which is required for its degradation by the E3 ubiquitin ligase complex SCF(Cdc4) (PubMed:12101234, PubMed:12455686). When associated with PCL9, may have a role in bud site selection in G1 phase (PubMed:9593297). PHO85 also phosphorylates the transcription factor SWI5 (PubMed:10692159). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10490639, ECO:0000269|PubMed:10692159, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11602261, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12006994, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12098764, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12101234, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12407105, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12455686, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12857883, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15057567, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15082539, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15598647, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15721288, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16308562, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16455487, ECO:0000269|PubMed:3067079, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7973730, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7973731, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8108735, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8539622, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9584169, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9593297, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9725902, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9843683}.

Merged_Functions: Encodes the mitochondrial malate dehydrogenase enzyme, which catalyzes the NAD⁺‑dependent oxidation of malate to oxaloacetate.  The enzyme functions as a dimer of identical subunits (~68 kDa) in the mitochondrial matrix and is a key component of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and the malate/aspartate shuttle.  Through these roles it provides an important mechanism for the exchange of substrates and reducing equivalents between central metabolic pathways that are separated by the mitochondrial membrane. {PubMed:3072021}. MDH1 encodes the mitochondrial malate dehydrogenase, a tricarboxylic‑acid (TCA) cycle enzyme required for respiratory metabolism of acetate. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, MDH1 activity is essential for the production of the extracellular meiosis‑promoting factor (MEP), which the authors identified as bicarbonate. Respiration‑competent cells use acetate, generate CO₂, and accumulate bicarbonate in the medium, raising extracellular pH and thereby stimulating the arrest of cell division and the induction of meiosis and sporulation. mdh1 mutant strains (mdh1‑2 and mdh1Δ) are unable to grow on acetate, fail to produce bicarbonate/MEP, and do not sporulate unless bicarbonate or other alkaline agents are supplied externally. Complementation with a plasmid bearing MDH1 restores acetate utilization, bicarbonate production, and normal sporulation. {PubMed:9639309}. MDH1 encodes the mitochondrial isozyme of malate dehydrogenase (MDH‑1).  This enzyme catalyzes the reversible oxidation of malate to oxaloacetate within the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, providing a key step for the oxidative metabolism of acetate in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.  Mutations in MDH1 result in reduced mitochondrial malate dehydrogenase activity and, in some alleles, loss of detectable MDH‑1 protein, leading to an acetate‑nonutilizing phenotype. {PubMed:8878673}. MDH1 is a mitochondrial isozyme of malate dehydrogenase that functions in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. It catalyzes the reversible interconversion of malate and oxaloacetate in conjunction with the conversion of NAD⁺ to NADH, thereby playing a role in carbohydrate and energy metabolism within mitochondria. {PubMed:30279312}.
Curated_Functions: Catalyzes the NAD⁺-dependent reversible oxidation of malate to oxaloacetate in the mitochondrial matrix. {PubMed:3072021, PubMed:8878673, PubMed:30279312}. Forms a homodimer of ~68 kDa subunits in the mitochondrial matrix. {PubMed:3072021}. Participates in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and the malate/aspartate shuttle, facilitating exchange of substrates and reducing equivalents between cytosolic and mitochondrial metabolic pathways. {PubMed:3072021}. Is required for respiratory metabolism of acetate. {PubMed:9639309, PubMed:8878673}. Is essential for production of the extracellular meiosis‑promoting factor (bicarbonate), thereby influencing extracellular pH, cell‑cycle arrest, and induction of meiosis and sporulation. {PubMed:9639309}. Mutations reduce mitochondrial malate dehydrogenase activity or abolish protein accumulation, leading to an acetate‑nonutilizing phenotype. {PubMed:8878673}.

Merged_Functions: TPM1 encodes a tropomyosin protein that binds to actin filaments and stabilizes actin cables in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.  NatB‑mediated N‑terminal acetylation of Tpm1 enhances its affinity for actin, promoting proper actin cable formation.  These actin cables serve as tracks for organelle segregation, vesicular transport, and endocytic trafficking during cell growth and division.  Overexpression of TPM1 (or a gain‑of‑function TPM1‑5 allele) can restore actin cable defects and suppress excess nicotinic acid/nicotinamide (NA/NAM) release in NatB mutants, although it does not rescue NAD⁺ levels. {PubMed:29317496}. TPM1 encodes the yeast tropomyosin 1 protein (Tpm1p), the only actin‑binding protein found exclusively on actin cables. Tpm1p binds directly to filamentous actin and is required to stabilize and properly orient actin cables throughout the cell cycle. Stabilized actin cables serve as tracks for the polarized, linear transport of mitochondria from mother cells into developing buds, and are also essential for polarized secretion, cell growth, shmoo formation, and cell fusion. Deletion of TPM1 (tpm1Δ) leads to selective loss of actin cables while leaving actin patches largely unaffected, resulting in abnormal mitochondrial morphology, reduced efficiency of mitochondrial inheritance, loss of long‑distance directional mitochondrial movement, and delayed transfer of mitochondria to buds. Thus, TPM1’s primary function is to maintain organized actin cable structures that are critical for directed organelle transport and other polarized cellular processes. {PubMed:9227850}. TPM1 encodes a tropomyosin protein that cooperates with TPM2 to stabilize cytoplasmic actin cables in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.  In the conditional double‑tropomyosin mutant (tpm1‑2 tpm2Δ), rapid loss of actin cables occurs after shifting to the restrictive temperature, while actin patches remain initially polarized.  The loss of cables caused by TPM1 dysfunction leads to a severe defect in polarized cell growth and secretion, mirroring the effects of actin depolymerization.  Thus, TPM1 is required for the formation/maintenance of actin cables, which are essential tracks for polarized transport of secretory vesicles and for proper polarized secretion. {PubMed:10793147}. TPM1 encodes a 199‑amino‑acid tropomyosin isoform in Saccharomyces cerevisiae that forms an elongated coiled‑coil dimer which binds longitudinally along actin filaments, spanning five actin monomers. The protein contains two four‑residue deletions (stammers) that interrupt the heptad repeat and flank a 38‑residue partial duplication unique to TPM1. By binding to actin, TPM1 stabilizes the filament and modulates actin‑myosin interactions: it alters the affinity of myosin S1 for actin (≈2.3‑fold increase), influences the cooperativity of myosin binding, and changes the concentration dependence of myosin‑driven filament sliding in vitro. Compared with the shorter TPM2 isoform, TPM1 produces greater steric hindrance to myosin, requires higher myosin concentrations for maximal sliding speed, and shifts the equilibrium of thin‑filament states toward a more resistant (C‑state) conformation. Overall, TPM1 functions as a non‑muscle tropomyosin that regulates thin‑filament structure, stability, and myosin motor activity in a isoform‑specific manner. {PubMed:11457840}. The TPM1 gene encodes non‑muscle tropomyosin isoforms (e.g., Tpm1.6 and Tpm1.8) that polymerize end‑to‑end along both strands of actin filaments. These isoforms stabilize actin filaments and protect them from cofilin‑induced severing and depolymerization. By binding to F‑actin, TPM1‑derived tropomyosins modulate the conformation of actin’s D‑loop and H‑loop, thereby altering longitudinal and lateral inter‑protomer contacts and regulating the activity of cofilin 1 (Cof1). Consequently, TPM1 products control actin filament dynamics, contributing to the structural integrity of stress fibers, contractile structures, and other cellular actin networks. {PubMed:31996302}. TPM1 encodes the yeast actin filament‑binding protein tropomyosin.  Tropomyosin is a rod‑shaped coiled‑coil dimer that binds along the groove of actin filaments and is required for the assembly and/or stabilization of actin cables.  In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, extra copies of TPM1 suppress the temperature‑sensitive growth and mitochondrial inheritance defects of mdm20 mutants and partially restore actin cables, indicating that TPM1 can compensate for loss of Mdm20p in maintaining functional actin structures.  Loss of TPM1 results in the disappearance of observable actin cables, growth retardation, cell size heterogeneity, multinucleate cells due to defects in mitotic spindle orientation, and severe nuclear segregation defects, although mitochondrial morphology and inheritance are only mildly affected.  TPM1 therefore functions as a key regulator of actin cable integrity, influencing processes such as mitochondrial transport into buds, nuclear segregation, and overall cell morphology. {PubMed:9105043}. MDM20 (YNL079C) encodes a novel ~93 kDa protein that is essential for mitochondrial inheritance during budding in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The protein is required for the formation and/or stabilization of actin cables; loss of MDM20 abolishes observable actin cables, which prevents the polarized transport of mitochondria into emerging buds while leaving mitochondrial morphology largely intact. MDM20 also genetically interacts with TPM1, BEM2, and MYO2 (synthetic lethality), supporting its role in an actin‑dependent pathway that coordinates actin cable integrity, organelle segregation, and bud growth. {PubMed:9105043}.

Provides tracks for polarized transport of mitochondria, secretory vesicles and other organelles, thereby supporting mitochondrial inheritance, polarized cell growth, secretion, shmoo formation, cell fusion and nuclear segregation. {PubMed:9227850, PubMed:10793147, PubMed:9105043}. Regulates thin‑filament structure and myosin motor activity, increasing myosin S1 affinity, influencing cooperativity and shifting the filament equilibrium toward a resistant C‑state. {PubMed:11457840}. Suppresses actin cable defects and excess nicotinic acid/nicotinamide release in NatB mutants when overexpressed. {PubMed:29317496}. Genetically interacts with MDM20, BEM2 and MYO2 in an actin‑dependent pathway that coordinates actin cable integrity, organelle segregation and bud growth. {PubMed:9105043}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Component of the Mediator complex, a coactivator involved in the regulated transcription of nearly all RNA polymerase II-dependent genes. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Transcription activator involved in oxidative stress response and redox homeostasis. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates. Component of RNA polymerase II which synthesizes mRNA precursors and many functional non-coding RNAs. Pol II is the central component of the basal RNA polymerase II transcription machinery. It is composed of mobile elements that move relative to each other. RPB4 is part of a subcomplex with RPB7 that binds to a pocket formed by RPB1, RPB2 and RPB6 at the base of the clamp element. The RPB4-RPB7 subcomplex seems to lock the clamp via RPB7 in the closed conformation thus preventing double-stranded DNA to enter the active site cleft. The RPB4-RPB7 subcomplex binds single-stranded DNA and RNA. The RPB4-RPB7 subcomplex is necessary for promoter-directed transcription initiation but is not required for recruitment of Pol II to active preinitiation complexes and seems to be dispensable for transcription elongation and termination. The RPB4-RPB7 subcomplex recruits FCP1 to Pol II. Involved in DNA repair of damage in the transcribed strand. RPB4 is dispensable under optimal growth conditions, but becomes essential during heat or cold shock and under nutrient depletion. Suppresses the RBP9-mediated transcription-coupled repair (TCR) subpathway of nucleotide excision repair (NER) but facilitates the RAD26-mediated TCR subpathway. Under stress conditions only, involved in mRNA export to the cytoplasm. Involved in mRNA decay. Promotes or enhances the deadenylation process of specific mRNAs and may recruit PAT1 and the LSM1-7 complex to these mRNAs, thus stimulating their decapping and further decay. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11087726, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11382749, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12411509, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12857861, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15304220, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16357218, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1985924}.

As one of the FG repeat nucleoporins NUP1 is involved in interactions with and guidance of nuclear transport receptors such as SRP1-KAP95 (importin alpha and beta) through the NPC. Like the closely related NUP2 it also plays an important role in disassembling and recycling SRP1-KAP95 to the cytoplasm after nuclear import. Upon entry of the heterotrimeric SRP1-KAP95-cargo complex in the nucleus, NUP1 binds through its C-terminus to KAP95, thus accelerating the release of KAP95 and, indirectly, of the nuclear localization signal (NLS)-containing cargo from the SRP1-KAP95-cargo complex. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10684247, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11046143, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11387327, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11535617, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11867631, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12372823, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12543930, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12604785, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12917401, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15039779}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Multifunctional protein that exhibits several independent functions at different levels of the cellular processes. 5'-3' exonuclease component of the nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) which is a highly conserved mRNA degradation pathway, an RNA surveillance system whose role is to identify and rid cells of mRNA with premature termination codons and thus prevents accumulation of potentially harmful truncated proteins. Acts as a microtubule-associated protein which interacts with cytoplasmic microtubules through beta-tubulin and promotes in vitro assembly of tubulin into microtubules. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Component of the ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase, a multisubunit transmembrane complex that is part of the mitochondrial electron transport chain which drives oxidative phosphorylation. The respiratory chain contains 3 multisubunit complexes succinate dehydrogenase (complex II, CII), ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase (cytochrome b-c1 complex, complex III, CIII) and cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV, CIV), that cooperate to transfer electrons derived from NADH and succinate to molecular oxygen, creating an electrochemical gradient over the inner membrane that drives transmembrane transport and the ATP synthase. The cytochrome b-c1 complex catalyzes electron transfer from ubiquinol to cytochrome c, linking this redox reaction to translocation of protons across the mitochondrial inner membrane, with protons being carried across the membrane as hydrogens on the quinol. In the process called Q cycle, 2 protons are consumed from the matrix, 4 protons are released into the intermembrane space and 2 electrons are passed to cytochrome c. {ECO:0000305|PubMed:11880631}.

FUNCTION: As part of the replication protein A (RPA/RP-A), a single-stranded DNA-binding heterotrimeric complex, may play an essential role in DNA replication, recombination and repair. Binds and stabilizes single-stranded DNA intermediates, preventing complementary DNA reannealing and recruiting different proteins involved in DNA metabolism. Binds to single-stranded sequences participating in DNA replication in addition to those mediating transcriptional repression (URS1) and activation (CAR1). Stimulates the activity of a cognate strand exchange protein (SEP1). It cooperates with T-AG and DNA topoisomerase I to unwind template DNA containing the simian virus 40 origin of DNA replication.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Sterol 24-C-methyltransferase; part of the third module of ergosterol biosynthesis pathway that includes the late steps of the pathway (PubMed:6363386). ERG6 catalyzes the methyl transfer from S-adenosyl-methionine to the C-24 of zymosterol to form fecosterol (PubMed:6363386). The third module or late pathway involves the ergosterol synthesis itself through consecutive reactions that mainly occur in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane. Firstly, the squalene synthase ERG9 catalyzes the condensation of 2 farnesyl pyrophosphate moieties to form squalene, which is the precursor of all steroids. Squalene synthase is crucial for balancing the incorporation of farnesyl diphosphate (FPP) into sterol and nonsterol isoprene synthesis. Secondly, the squalene epoxidase ERG1 catalyzes the stereospecific oxidation of squalene to (S)-2,3-epoxysqualene, which is considered to be a rate-limiting enzyme in steroid biosynthesis. Then, the lanosterol synthase ERG7 catalyzes the cyclization of (S)-2,3 oxidosqualene to lanosterol, a reaction that forms the sterol core. In the next steps, lanosterol is transformed to zymosterol through a complex process involving various demethylation, reduction and desaturation reactions. The lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase ERG11 (also known as CYP51) catalyzes C14-demethylation of lanosterol to produce 4,4'-dimethyl cholesta-8,14,24-triene-3-beta-ol, which is critical for ergosterol biosynthesis. The C-14 reductase ERG24 reduces the C14=C15 double bond of 4,4-dimethyl-cholesta-8,14,24-trienol to produce 4,4-dimethyl-cholesta-8,24-dienol. 4,4-dimethyl-cholesta-8,24-dienol is substrate of the C-4 demethylation complex ERG25-ERG26-ERG27 in which ERG25 catalyzes the three-step monooxygenation required for the demethylation of 4,4-dimethyl and 4alpha-methylsterols, ERG26 catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation that results in a reduction of the 3-beta-hydroxy group at the C-3 carbon to an oxo group, and ERG27 is responsible for the reduction of the keto group on the C-3. ERG28 has a role as a scaffold to help anchor ERG25, ERG26 and ERG27 to the endoplasmic reticulum and ERG29 regulates the activity of the iron-containing C4-methylsterol oxidase ERG25. Then, the sterol 24-C-methyltransferase ERG6 catalyzes the methyl transfer from S-adenosyl-methionine to the C-24 of zymosterol to form fecosterol. The C-8 sterol isomerase ERG2 catalyzes the reaction which results in unsaturation at C-7 in the B ring of sterols and thus converts fecosterol to episterol. The sterol-C5-desaturase ERG3 then catalyzes the introduction of a C-5 double bond in the B ring to produce 5-dehydroepisterol. The C-22 sterol desaturase ERG5 further converts 5-dehydroepisterol into ergosta-5,7,22,24(28)-tetraen-3beta-ol by forming the C-22(23) double bond in the sterol side chain. Finally, ergosta-5,7,22,24(28)-tetraen-3beta-ol is substrate of the C-24(28) sterol reductase ERG4 to produce ergosterol (PubMed:32679672). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:6363386, ECO:0000303|PubMed:32679672}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Component of the post-replicative DNA mismatch repair system (MMR). Heterodimerizes with MSH2 to form MutS beta, which binds to DNA mismatches thereby initiating DNA repair. MSH3 provides substrate-binding and substrate specificity to the complex. When bound, the MutS beta heterodimer bends the DNA helix and shields approximately 20 base pairs. Acts mainly to repair insertion-deletion loops (IDLs) from 2 to 13 nucleotides in size, but can also repair base-base and single insertion-deletion mismatches that occur during replication. After mismatch binding, forms a ternary complex with either the MutL alpha or MutL beta heterodimer, which is thought to be responsible for directing the downstream MMR events, including strand discrimination, excision, and resynthesis. MutS beta also has a role in regulation of heteroduplex formation during mitotic and meiotic recombination. MutS beta binds to DNA flap structures predicted to form during recombination, and is required for 3' non-homologous tail removal (NHTR). MutS beta-binding alters the DNA conformation of its substrate at the ds/ssDNA junction and may facilitate its recognition and/or cleavage by the downstream nucleotide excision repair (NER) RAD1-RAD10 endonuclease. ATP binding and hydrolysis play a pivotal role in MMR and NHTR. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:16702432, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16781730, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17157869, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17573527, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17636021, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8600025, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9111357, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9256462, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9368761, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9770499}.

FUNCTION: C-24(28) sterol reductase; part of the third module of ergosterol biosynthesis pathway that includes the late steps of the pathway (PubMed:10722850, PubMed:12882006, PubMed:8125337). ERG4 Catalyzes the last step of ergosterol biosynthesis by converting ergosta-5,7,22,24(28)-tetraen-3beta-ol into ergosterol (PubMed:10722850, PubMed:12882006). The third module or late pathway involves the ergosterol synthesis itself through consecutive reactions that mainly occur in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane. Firstly, the squalene synthase ERG9 catalyzes the condensation of 2 farnesyl pyrophosphate moieties to form squalene, which is the precursor of all steroids. Squalene synthase is crucial for balancing the incorporation of farnesyl diphosphate (FPP) into sterol and nonsterol isoprene synthesis. Secondly, the squalene epoxidase ERG1 catalyzes the stereospecific oxidation of squalene to (S)-2,3-epoxysqualene, which is considered to be a rate-limiting enzyme in steroid biosynthesis. Then, the lanosterol synthase ERG7 catalyzes the cyclization of (S)-2,3 oxidosqualene to lanosterol, a reaction that forms the sterol core. In the next steps, lanosterol is transformed to zymosterol through a complex process involving various demethylation, reduction and desaturation reactions. The lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase ERG11 (also known as CYP51) catalyzes C14-demethylation of lanosterol to produce 4,4'-dimethyl cholesta-8,14,24-triene-3-beta-ol, which is critical for ergosterol biosynthesis. The C-14 reductase ERG24 reduces the C14=C15 double bond of 4,4-dimethyl-cholesta-8,14,24-trienol to produce 4,4-dimethyl-cholesta-8,24-dienol. 4,4-dimethyl-cholesta-8,24-dienol is substrate of the C-4 demethylation complex ERG25-ERG26-ERG27 in which ERG25 catalyzes the three-step monooxygenation required for the demethylation of 4,4-dimethyl and 4alpha-methylsterols, ERG26 catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation that results in a reduction of the 3-beta-hydroxy group at the C-3 carbon to an oxo group, and ERG27 is responsible for the reduction of the keto group on the C-3. ERG28 has a role as a scaffold to help anchor ERG25, ERG26 and ERG27 to the endoplasmic reticulum and ERG29 regulates the activity of the iron-containing C4-methylsterol oxidase ERG25. Then, the sterol 24-C-methyltransferase ERG6 catalyzes the methyl transfer from S-adenosyl-methionine to the C-24 of zymosterol to form fecosterol. The C-8 sterol isomerase ERG2 catalyzes the reaction which results in unsaturation at C-7 in the B ring of sterols and thus converts fecosterol to episterol. The sterol-C5-desaturase ERG3 then catalyzes the introduction of a C-5 double bond in the B ring to produce 5-dehydroepisterol. The C-22 sterol desaturase ERG5 further converts 5-dehydroepisterol into ergosta-5,7,22,24(28)-tetraen-3beta-ol by forming the C-22(23) double bond in the sterol side chain. Finally, ergosta-5,7,22,24(28)-tetraen-3beta-ol is substrate of the C-24(28) sterol reductase ERG4 to produce ergosterol (PubMed:32679672). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10722850, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12882006, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8125337, ECO:0000303|PubMed:32679672}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Septins are GTPases involved in cytokinesis that assemble early in the cell cycle as a patch at the incipient bud site and form a ring approximate 15 minutes before bud emergence, which transforms into an hour-glass shaped collar of cortical filaments that spans both sides of the mother-bud neck. This collar persists until just before cytokinesis, when it splits into two rings that occupy opposite sides of the neck. The septins at the bud neck serve as a structural scaffold that recruits different components involved in diverse processes at specific stages during the cell cycle. Many proteins bind asymmetrically to the septin collar. The septin assembly is regulated by protein kinases GIN4 and/or CLA4. May act by recruiting MYO1 and HOF1, a protein involved in septation, to the site of cleavage. Septins are also involved in cell morphogenesis, bud site selection, chitin deposition, cell cycle regulation, cell compartmentalization and spore wall formation.

Merged_Functions: YCP4 encodes a flavodoxin‑like protein that acts as a regulator of gene expression during the late stages of growth in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. It positively influences SPI1 promoter activity in post‑diauxic and stationary phases and, together with its homolog RFS1, modulates a broad transcriptional program: it represses genes involved in carbon metabolism (high‑affinity glucose transporters, hexokinases, glycolytic enzymes) and activates genes linked to nitrogen/amino‑acid metabolism and mating‑pheromone response. Deletion of YCP4 (especially in combination with RFS1) alters stress tolerance—enhancing resistance to oxidative stress (via increased catalase CTT1 activity) while affecting sensitivity to osmotic stress and cell‑wall damaging agents (SDS). The double mutant also shows altered chronological lifespan (short‑term increase, long‑term decrease) and a modest rise in fermentative capacity. Ycp4 localizes to punctate cytoplasmic foci (no nuclear co‑localization) and likely participates in an early signaling or post‑transcriptional regulatory pathway rather than acting as a classical transcription factor. {PubMed:21442317}. Ycp4 is a Saccharomyces cerevisiae protein of previously unknown function that contains a flavodoxin‑like (Flavodoxin_1) domain. In the context of this study, Ycp4 was identified as a regulator of the redox state of human PTEN expressed in yeast. Deletion of YCP4 (ycp4Δ) caused a noticeable delay in the reduction of H₂O₂‑oxidized hPTEN, indicating that Ycp4 facilitates the conversion of oxidized PTEN back to its reduced, active form. Reintroduction of YCP4 into the mutant restored normal PTEN reduction kinetics and rescued the slight growth defect of the ycp4Δ strain. Although no human ortholog has been definitively identified, Ycp4 is reported to be present in highly purified mitochondria, suggesting a mitochondrial role in redox processes that impact PTEN reduction. {PubMed:21371429}. The article reports that YCP4, originally identified in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, has no known biochemical function. Sequence analysis of YCP4 and its two homologs shows no hydrophobic domains or targeting signals, indicating that it is most likely a soluble cytoplasmic protein. It is described as a non‑essential gene product and is presumed to reside in the cytoplasm, similar to the other fungal allergens characterized in the study. {PubMed:7898496}. YCP4 encodes a flavodoxin‑like protein that belongs to the WrbA family of FMN‑binding quinone reductases.  Members of this family are induced under heat‑shock and oxidative‑stress conditions and function to reduce quinones, thereby preventing the formation of reactive semiquinone radicals.  YCP4 therefore participates in cellular defenses against oxidative stress and may also have a DNA‑binding (helix‑turn‑helix) role associated with stress‑responsive transcriptional regulation. {PubMed:15809007}. YCP4 encodes a flavodoxin‑like protein that is a member of a small family of putative NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductases in yeast.  Sequence analysis shows it is homologous to the bacterial WrbA quinone reductase and contains the conserved active‑site residues characteristic of two‑electron quinone reductases.  Functional assays demonstrated that deletion of YCP4 makes cells hypersensitive to hydroquinone (HQ) but not to catechol (CAT), and confers resistance to 1,2,4‑benzenetriol (BT).  Overexpression of YCP4 increases sensitivity to all three benzene metabolites, consistent with a role in modulating quinone redox cycling.  The authors therefore propose that Ycp4p catalyzes the NAD(P)H‑dependent two‑electron reduction of para‑quinones (e.g., 1,4‑benzoquinone derived from HQ), thereby contributing to cellular detoxification and tolerance of hydroquinone stress. {PubMed:21912624}. YCR004C encodes the flavodoxin‑like protein Ycp4.  Ycp4 acts as a positive regulator of the SPI1 promoter during the late stages of growth (post‑diauxic and stationary phases) and, together with its homolog Rfs1, modulates the expression of a broad set of genes.  Deletion of YCR004C (ycp4Δ) reduces SPI1 induction and, when combined with an rfs1Δ deletion, leads to up‑regulation of genes involved in carbohydrate metabolism (hexose transporters, glycolytic enzymes) and down‑regulation of genes related to mating, pheromone response, and amino‑acid biosynthesis, indicating that Ycp4 represses carbon‑metabolism genes and promotes nitrogen‑metabolism genes.  Ycp4 also contributes to stress tolerance: single mutants show normal oxidative stress resistance, while the ycp4Δ rfs1Δ double mutant displays increased resistance to hydrogen peroxide, altered sensitivity to osmotic stress (KCl) and cell‑wall damage (SDS), and changes in catalase activity.  Additionally, the double mutant exhibits a modest increase in fermentative capacity, an altered chronological lifespan (enhanced short‑term but reduced long‑term survival), and a punctate cytoplasmic localization that does not change in stationary phase.  Overall, YCR004C/Ycp4 functions as a flavodoxin‑like regulator of gene expression affecting metabolism, stress responses, and aging in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. {PubMed:21442317}. The article identifies YCR004C as the YCP4 gene, a protein of unknown precise biochemical activity that contains a flavodoxin-like domain and is detected in mitochondria. Deletion of YCR004C (ycp4Δ) delays the cellular reduction of oxidized human PTEN (hPTEN) after H₂O₂ treatment, indicating that YCP4 participates in the redox regulation of PTEN. Restoration of YCR004C expression in a revertant strain rescues both the growth defect of the mutant and the delayed PTEN reduction, confirming its role. While the exact mechanism is not defined, the data suggest that YCP4 functions as a mitochondrial factor that facilitates the reduction of oxidized PTEN, possibly through a flavodoxin-associated redox process. {PubMed:21371429}. The article refers to YCR004C as the Saccharomyces cerevisiae YCP4 gene. It states that YCP4 encodes a protein of unknown function; the protein lacks hydrophobic domains or targeting signals, suggesting it is a soluble cytoplasmic protein. It is described as a non‑essential gene and a member of a small “YCP4 family” of proteins conserved in fungi, but no specific biochemical activity or cellular role is reported. {PubMed:7898496}. The article identifies YCR004C as the budding‑yeast protein Ycp4, a member of the WrbA family. No experimental functional characterization has been reported; it is described as a protein of unknown function. Ycp4 contains a C‑terminal extension bearing signals for farnesylation and carboxy‑methylation. The authors note that upstream of the Ycp4 open reading frame there are AP‑1‑like promoter elements, suggesting regulation by the PAR1 transcription factor and a possible involvement in oxidative‑stress responses, analogous to the regulation of the fission‑yeast P25 protein. However, the precise biochemical role of YCR004C remains undefined. {PubMed:7756978}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Non-catalytic component of the RNA exosome complex which has 3'->5' exoribonuclease activity and participates in a multitude of cellular RNA processing and degradation events. In the nucleus, the RNA exosome complex is involved in proper maturation of stable RNA species such as rRNA, snRNA and snoRNA, in the elimination of RNA processing by-products and non-coding 'pervasive' transcripts, such as antisense RNA species and cryptic unstable transcripts (CUTs), and of mRNAs with processing defects, thereby limiting or excluding their export to the cytoplasm. In the cytoplasm, the RNA exosome complex is involved in general mRNA turnover and in RNA surveillance pathways, preventing translation of aberrant mRNAs. The catalytic inactive RNA exosome core complex of 9 subunits (Exo-9) is proposed to play a pivotal role in the binding and presentation of RNA for ribonucleolysis, and to serve as a scaffold for the association with catalytic subunits and accessory proteins or complexes. RRP43 is part of the hexameric ring of RNase PH domain-containing subunits proposed to form a central channel which threads RNA substrates for degradation. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:12364597, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17173052, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9390555, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9973615}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Component of the ribosome, a large ribonucleoprotein complex responsible for the synthesis of proteins in the cell. The small ribosomal subunit (SSU) binds messenger RNAs (mRNAs) and translates the encoded message by selecting cognate aminoacyl-transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules. The large subunit (LSU) contains the ribosomal catalytic site termed the peptidyl transferase center (PTC), which catalyzes the formation of peptide bonds, thereby polymerizing the amino acids delivered by tRNAs into a polypeptide chain. The nascent polypeptides leave the ribosome through a tunnel in the LSU and interact with protein factors that function in enzymatic processing, targeting, and the membrane insertion of nascent chains at the exit of the ribosomal tunnel (PubMed:22096102). uS5 is important for the assembly and function of the 40S ribosomal subunit. Mutations in this protein affects the control of translational fidelity. Involved in nucleolar processing of pre-18S ribosomal RNA and ribosome assembly (PubMed:15590835). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:15590835, ECO:0000305|PubMed:22096102}.

FUNCTION: Chromatin reader component of the transcription coactivator SAGA complex. SAGA acts as a general cofactor required for essentially all RNA polymerase II transcription (PubMed:10026213, PubMed:10864329, PubMed:15647753, PubMed:25216679, PubMed:28918903). At the promoters, SAGA is required for transcription pre-initiation complex (PIC) recruitment. It influences RNA polymerase II transcriptional activity through different activities such as TBP interaction (via core/TAF module) and promoter selectivity, interaction with transcription activators (via Tra1/SPT module), and chromatin modification through histone acetylation (via HAT module) and deubiquitination (via DUB module) (PubMed:22224423). SAGA preferentially acetylates histones H3 (to form H3K9ac, H3K14ac, H3K18ac and H3K23ac) and H2B and deubiquitinates histone H2B (PubMed:10026213). SAGA interacts with DNA via upstream activating sequences (UASs) (PubMed:28918903). Also identified in a modified version of SAGA named SALSA or SLIK (PubMed:15647753). The cleavage of SPT7 and the absence of the SPT8 subunit in SLIK neither drive any major conformational differences in its structure compared with SAGA, nor significantly affect HAT, DUB, or DNA-binding activities (PubMed:33864814). SGF29 specifically recognizes and binds methylated 'Lys-4' of histone H3 (H3K4me), with a preference for trimethylated form (H3K4me3) (PubMed:21685874). Component of the ADA histone acetyltransferase complex, which preferentially acetylates nucleosomal histones H3 (to form H3K14ac and H3K18ac) and H2B (PubMed:10026213). SGF29 is also required for heterochromatin boundary formation function, prevention of the spread of gene silencing at the HMR locus (PubMed:24307402). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10026213, ECO:0000269|PubMed:10864329, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15647753, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21685874, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22224423, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24307402, ECO:0000269|PubMed:25216679, ECO:0000269|PubMed:28918903, ECO:0000269|PubMed:33864814}.

FUNCTION: Component of the post-replicative DNA mismatch repair system (MMR). Forms two different heterodimers: MutS alpha (MSH2-MSH6 heterodimer) and MutS beta (MSH2-MSH3 heterodimer), which bind to DNA mismatches thereby initiating DNA repair. MSH2 seems to act as a scaffold for the other MutS homologs that provide substrate-binding and substrate specificity. When bound, heterodimers bend the DNA helix and shield approximately 20 base pairs. MutS alpha acts mainly to repair base-base and single insertion-deletion mismatches that occur during replication, but can also repair longer insertion-deletion loops (IDLs), although with decreasing efficiency as the size of the extrahelical loop increases. MutS beta acts mainly to repair IDLs from 2 to 13 nucleotides in size, but can also repair base-base and single insertion-deletion mismatches. After mismatch binding, MutS alpha or beta form a ternary complex with a MutL heterodimer, which is thought to be responsible for directing the downstream MMR events, including strand discrimination, excision, and resynthesis. ATP binding and hydrolysis play a pivotal role in mismatch repair functions. Both subunits bind ATP, but with differing affinities, and their ATPase kinetics are also very different. MSH6 binds and hydrolyzes ATP rapidly, whereas MSH2 catalyzes ATP at a substantially slower rate. Binding to a mismatched base pair suppresses MSH6-catalyzed ATP hydrolysis, but not the activity of MSH2. ATP binding to both subunits is necessary to trigger a change in MutS alpha interaction with mismatched DNA, converting MutS alpha into a sliding clamp capable of hydrolysis-independent movement along DNA, and also facilitates formation of ternary complexes containing MutS and MutL proteins and the mismatch. MutS beta also has a role in regulation of heteroduplex formation during mitotic and meiotic recombination. MutS beta binds to DNA flap structures predicted to form during recombination, and is required for 3' non-homologous tail removal (NHTR). MutS beta-binding alters the DNA conformation of its substrate at the ds/ssDNA junction and may facilitate its recognition and/or cleavage by the downstream nucleotide excision repair (NER) RAD1-RAD10 endonuclease. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10518225, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11237611, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12509278, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12820877, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12875840, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15811858, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16214425, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16337600, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16600868, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16702432, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16781730, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17157869, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17636021, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8600025, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9111357, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9256462, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9368761, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9545323, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9770499}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Minor of three pyruvate decarboxylases (PDC1, PDC5, PDC6) implicated in the nonoxidative conversion of pyruvate to acetaldehyde and carbon dioxide during alcoholic fermentation. Most of the produced acetaldehyde is subsequently reduced to ethanol, but some is required for cytosolic acetyl-CoA production for biosynthetic pathways. The enzyme is also one of five 2-oxo acid decarboxylases (PDC1, PDC5, PDC6, ARO10, and THI3) able to decarboxylate more complex 2-oxo acids (alpha-keto-acids) than pyruvate, which seem mainly involved in amino acid catabolism. Here the enzyme catalyzes the decarboxylation of amino acids, which, in a first step, have been transaminated to the corresponding 2-oxo acids. In a third step, the resulting aldehydes are reduced to alcohols, collectively referred to as fusel oils or alcohols. Its preferred substrates are the transaminated amino acids derived from threonine (2-oxobutanoate), norvaline (2-oxopentanoate), valine (3-methyl-2-oxobutanoate, also alpha-keto-isovalerate), isoleucine ((3S)-3-methyl-2-oxopentanoate, also alpha-keto-beta-methylvalerate), phenylalanine (phenylpyruvate), and tryptophan (3-(indol-3-yl)pyruvate), whereas transaminated leucine is no substrate. In a side-reaction the carbanionic intermediate (or active aldehyde) generated by decarboxylation or by activation of an aldehyde can react with an aldehyde via condensation (or carboligation) yielding a 2-hydroxy ketone, collectively called acyloins. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Activator protein that regulates the ubiquitin ligase activity and substrate specificity of the anaphase promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C). FUNCTION: Component of the ribosome, a large ribonucleoprotein complex responsible for the synthesis of proteins in the cell. FUNCTION: Component of the mitochondrial ribosome (mitoribosome), a dedicated translation machinery responsible for the synthesis of mitochondrial genome-encoded proteins, including at least some of the essential transmembrane subunits of the mitochondrial respiratory chain. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Squalene synthase; part of the third module of ergosterol biosynthesis pathway that includes the late steps of the pathway (PubMed:1807826, PubMed:2068081, PubMed:8323279, PubMed:9742963). ERG9 produces squalene from 2 farnesyl pyrophosphate moieties (PubMed:1807826, PubMed:8323279). The third module or late pathway involves the ergosterol synthesis itself through consecutive reactions that mainly occur in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane. Firstly, the squalene synthase ERG9 catalyzes the condensation of 2 farnesyl pyrophosphate moieties to form squalene, which is the precursor of all steroids. Squalene synthase is crucial for balancing the incorporation of farnesyl diphosphate (FPP) into sterol and nonsterol isoprene synthesis. Secondly, the squalene epoxidase ERG1 catalyzes the stereospecific oxidation of squalene to (S)-2,3-epoxysqualene, which is considered to be a rate-limiting enzyme in steroid biosynthesis. Then, the lanosterol synthase ERG7 catalyzes the cyclization of (S)-2,3 oxidosqualene to lanosterol, a reaction that forms the sterol core. In the next steps, lanosterol is transformed to zymosterol through a complex process involving various demethylation, reduction and desaturation reactions. The lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase ERG11 (also known as CYP51) catalyzes C14-demethylation of lanosterol to produce 4,4'-dimethyl cholesta-8,14,24-triene-3-beta-ol, which is critical for ergosterol biosynthesis. The C-14 reductase ERG24 reduces the C14=C15 double bond of 4,4-dimethyl-cholesta-8,14,24-trienol to produce 4,4-dimethyl-cholesta-8,24-dienol. 4,4-dimethyl-cholesta-8,24-dienol is substrate of the C-4 demethylation complex ERG25-ERG26-ERG27 in which ERG25 catalyzes the three-step monooxygenation required for the demethylation of 4,4-dimethyl and 4alpha-methylsterols, ERG26 catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation that results in a reduction of the 3-beta-hydroxy group at the C-3 carbon to an oxo group, and ERG27 is responsible for the reduction of the keto group on the C-3. ERG28 has a role as a scaffold to help anchor ERG25, ERG26 and ERG27 to the endoplasmic reticulum and ERG29 regulates the activity of the iron-containing C4-methylsterol oxidase ERG25. Then, the sterol 24-C-methyltransferase ERG6 catalyzes the methyl transfer from S-adenosyl-methionine to the C-24 of zymosterol to form fecosterol. The C-8 sterol isomerase ERG2 catalyzes the reaction which results in unsaturation at C-7 in the B ring of sterols and thus converts fecosterol to episterol. The sterol-C5-desaturase ERG3 then catalyzes the introduction of a C-5 double bond in the B ring to produce 5-dehydroepisterol. The C-22 sterol desaturase ERG5 further converts 5-dehydroepisterol into ergosta-5,7,22,24(28)-tetraen-3beta-ol by forming the C-22(23) double bond in the sterol side chain. Finally, ergosta-5,7,22,24(28)-tetraen-3beta-ol is substrate of the C-24(28) sterol reductase ERG4 to produce ergosterol (PubMed:32679672). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:1807826, ECO:0000269|PubMed:2068081, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8323279, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9742963, ECO:0000303|PubMed:32679672}.

FUNCTION: Mitochondrial membrane ATP synthase (F(1)F(0) ATP synthase or Complex V) produces ATP from ADP in the presence of a proton gradient across the membrane which is generated by electron transport complexes of the respiratory chain. F-type ATPases consist of two structural domains, F(1) - containing the extramembraneous catalytic core, and F(0) - containing the membrane proton channel, linked together by a central stalk and a peripheral stalk. During catalysis, ATP synthesis in the catalytic domain of F(1) is coupled via a rotary mechanism of the central stalk subunits to proton translocation. Part of the complex F(0) domain and the peripheric stalk, which acts as a stator to hold the catalytic alpha(3)beta(3) subcomplex and subunit a/ATP6 static relative to the rotary elements.

FUNCTION: Malate synthase which takes part in the glyoxylate cycle (PubMed:1454530). MLS1 activity is essential for cells to grow on oleic acid as a sole carbon source (PubMed:11846793). Two steps of the glyoxylate cycle take place in the cytosol, the splitting of isocitrate into succinate and glyoxylate, and the dehydrogenation of malate to oxaloacetate (PubMed:1454530). However, the formation of malate from glyoxylate and acetyl-CoA undertaken MLS1, occurs in the peroxisomes when cells are grown on oleic acid (Probable). The source of acetyl-CoA being either peroxisomal when breaking down fatty acids, or cytosolic when extra-cellular two-carbon substrates are used, therefore, although not strictly essential, the peroxisomal localization of MLS1 appears to be advantageous for cells growing on oleic acid, in that acetyl-CoA production and utilization are thereby intimately compartmentalized together to increase efficiency (Probable). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11846793, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1454530, ECO:0000305|PubMed:1454530}.

FUNCTION: Subunit of the V1 complex of vacuolar(H+)-ATPase (V-ATPase), a multisubunit enzyme composed of a peripheral complex (V1) that hydrolyzes ATP and a membrane integral complex (V0) that translocates protons (PubMed:10781598, PubMed:11777935, PubMed:1730668, PubMed:8416931). Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Component of the Mediator complex, a coactivator involved in the regulated transcription of nearly all RNA polymerase II-dependent genes. Mediator functions as a bridge to convey information from gene-specific regulatory proteins to the basal RNA polymerase II transcription machinery. The Mediator complex, having a compact conformation in its free form, is recruited to promoters by direct interactions with regulatory proteins and serves for the assembly of a functional preinitiation complex with RNA polymerase II and the general transcription factors. The Mediator complex unfolds to an extended conformation and partially surrounds RNA polymerase II, specifically interacting with the unphosphorylated form of the C-terminal domain (CTD) of RNA polymerase II. The Mediator complex dissociates from the RNA polymerase II holoenzyme and stays at the promoter when transcriptional elongation begins. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:16076843, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16109375, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16263706}.

Plays a role in the maintenance and remodeling of mitochondrial cristae, some invaginations of the mitochondrial inner membrane that provide an increase in the surface area (PubMed:31292547). Merged_Functions: Encodes the glutamine synthetase Gln1, a GSII‑type enzyme that catalyzes the ATP‑dependent condensation of glutamate and ammonium to form glutamine. Gln1 assembles into pentameric rings that stack into decamers and can further associate via a novel back‑to‑back pentamer interface to create a nanotube‑like supramolecular assembly. Citrate binds the active site (interacting with Glu193, Gln198, Gly246, His250, Arg292), suggesting a competitive inhibition mechanism, and a flexible segment (Leu293‑Ala300) may act as a gate for glutamate entry to the active site. {PubMed:19322816}. Encodes the enzyme glutamine synthetase, which catalyzes the ATP‑dependent condensation of ammonia with glutamate to produce glutamine. This reaction is a key step in the assimilation of inorganic nitrogen, providing glutamine for protein synthesis and as a nitrogen donor for the synthesis of other amino acids, nucleotides, and polysaccharides. The GLN1 (YPR035W) protein is a 370‑amino‑acid polypeptide (~41.7 kDa) that forms a multimeric enzyme complex. Its expression is tightly regulated at the transcriptional level by three systems: (1) a strong response to a shift from glutamine to glutamate as the nitrogen source mediated by the GLN3/URE2 pathway, (2) a weaker response to purine starvation, and (3) a modest response to general amino‑acid control via GCN4. {PubMed:1347768}. Encodes the Saccharomyces cerevisiae glutamine synthetase Gln1, a GSII‑type enzyme (EC 6.3.1.2) that catalyzes the ATP‑dependent condensation of glutamate and ammonium to produce glutamine. The enzyme participates in nitrogen assimilation by converting toxic ammonia into the non‑toxic amino acid glutamine. Structurally, Gln1 forms pentameric rings that stack into decamers and can further associate into a nanotube‑like supramolecular assembly, but its primary biochemical role is the synthesis of glutamine from glutamate and NH₄⁺. {PubMed:19322816}. GLN1 encodes the yeast glutamine synthetase enzyme. The enzyme catalyzes the ATP‑dependent condensation of ammonia with glutamate to produce glutamine, thereby providing the primary route for assimilation of inorganic nitrogen into organic compounds. Glutamine generated by GLN1 serves as a direct nitrogen source for protein synthesis and as a nitrogen donor for the biosynthesis of other amino acids, nucleotides, and polysaccharides. The GLN1 protein is a 370‑amino‑acid polypeptide (~42 kDa) that assembles into a multimeric complex of 10–12 subunits. In addition to its catalytic role, the article describes that GLN1 expression is tightly regulated at the transcriptional level by three systems: (1) a nitrogen‑source response mediated by the GLN3/URE2 pathway that increases transcription when cells shift from glutamine to glutamate; (2) a purine‑starvation response; and (3) a general amino‑acid control pathway (GCN4). The upstream region of GLN1 contains distinct cis‑acting elements for these regulatory inputs. {PubMed:1347768}. The article mentions GLN1 (also referred to as Gln1p) as a gene whose product participates in the uptake of glutamine (and also asparagine). It is listed among the permeases (Agp1p, Gln1p, Dip5p, Gap1p) that can transport glutamine, and it is noted that GLN1 is not transcriptionally induced on a non‑repressive nitrogen source, unlike AGP1. {PubMed:10654085}. GLN1 encodes the yeast glutamine synthetase (GSII) enzyme. According to the article, glutamine synthetase (EC 6.3.1.2) catalyzes the condensation of glutamate and ammonium to produce glutamine, coupled with the hydrolysis of ATP. The protein functions in nitrogen metabolism by assimilating free ammonia into the non‑toxic amino acid glutamine. The study further characterizes GLN1 as a decameric GSII that can assemble into higher‑order nanotube‑like supramolecular structures, and notes that citrate can bind to the active site and potentially inhibit its activity. {PubMed:19322816}. GLN1 encodes the yeast glutamine synthetase enzyme, which catalyzes the ATP‑dependent synthesis of glutamine from glutamate and ammonium. The enzyme is the primary cellular target of the inhibitors L‑methionine sulfoximine (MSO) and the phytotoxin tabtoxin; inhibition of GLN1 activity leads to growth arrest. Overexpression of GLN1 from a multicopy plasmid raises cellular glutamine synthetase levels several‑fold, thereby increasing resistance to both MSO and tabtoxin. Thus, GLN1 functions in nitrogen metabolism by providing the major route for glutamine biosynthesis and determines cellular sensitivity to compounds that inhibit glutamine synthetase. {PubMed:2884208}. GLN1 encodes the enzyme glutamine synthetase, which catalyzes the synthesis of glutamine from glutamate and ammonia. Its transcription is tightly regulated by nitrogen availability: expression is repressed when glutamine is present in the growth medium and induced when cells are grown on glutamate or other nitrogen sources that do not raise intracellular glutamine levels. Activation of GLN1 transcription requires the upstream activation sequence (UAS‑N) containing a GATAAG element that is bound by the transcription factor Gln3p (and, to a lesser extent, by Nil1p). Deletion of the GATAAG element markedly reduces GLN1 expression. Thus, GLN1 functions as a key component of nitrogen metabolism, providing glutamine for cellular processes and being controlled by nitrogen‑responsive transcription factors. {PubMed:7568152}. GLN1 encodes the enzyme glutamine synthetase (GS), which catalyzes the ATP‑dependent incorporation of ammonium ion into glutamate to form glutamine, a key step in nitrogen assimilation in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The gene’s transcription is regulated by the nitrogen‑responsive transcription factor Gln3p (repressed by Ure2p in the presence of ammonia or glutamine) and also by the general amino‑acid control regulator Gcn4p. In the experiments described, GLN1 mRNA levels remained constant across a range of dilution rates, while GS enzymatic activity increased with higher dilution rates, indicating post‑transcriptional (e.g., translational or allosteric) regulation. Thus, GLN1 functions to provide glutamine for cellular metabolism and its activity is modulated in response to changes in extracellular ammonia concentration and carbon/nitrogen fluxes. {PubMed:7773405}. GLN1 encodes the glutamine synthetase enzyme in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, which catalyzes the synthesis of glutamine from glutamate (and ammonium). This reaction provides the glutamine required as a nitrogen donor for the first and fourth steps of de novo purine biosynthesis. {PubMed:9749667}.

Provides glutamine as a nitrogen donor for protein synthesis and for the biosynthesis of other amino acids, nucleotides and polysaccharides. {PubMed:1347768, PubMed:9749667}. Transports glutamine and asparagine across the plasma membrane. {PubMed:10654085}. Serves as the primary cellular target of L‑methionine sulfoximine and tabtoxin; inhibition causes growth arrest, and overexpression confers resistance to these compounds. {PubMed:2884208}. Is transcriptionally activated by nitrogen‑source signaling through the GLN3/URE2 pathway, by purine starvation, and by general amino‑acid control via GCN4. {PubMed:1347768, PubMed:7568152, PubMed:7773405}. Requires the upstream activation sequence UAS‑N containing a GATAAG element bound by Gln3p (and Nil1p) for full transcriptional activation. {PubMed:7568152}. Exhibits post‑transcriptional regulation: enzymatic activity increases with growth rate despite constant mRNA levels, indicating translational or allosteric control. {PubMed:7773405}. Supplies glutamine as the nitrogen donor for the first and fourth steps of de novo purine biosynthesis. {PubMed:9749667}.

FUNCTION: Plasma membrane signaling mucin that promotes activation of the MAPK for the filamentous growth pathway. FUNCTION: Has a dual role in the assembly of cytochrome oxidase subunit 1 (COX1). It has a regulative function on COX1 synthesis, acting as a translational activator specific for the COX1 mRNA, and it also binds to newly synthesized COX1 protein. Together with COX14, may act as a chaperone that binds efficiently unassembled COX1 and prevents it from unproductive aggregation. When bound to COX1, MSS51 is unable to interact with the COX1 mRNA and translation is halted. This may be a feedback control that ensures that COX1 is only produced as long as potentially harmful assembly intermediates are not accumulating. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10803883, ECO:0000269|PubMed:14592991, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15306853, ECO:0000269|PubMed:6320175}.

FUNCTION: Involved in astral microtubule organization by binding SCP72 to the outer plaque in a cell-cycle dependent manner. Required for the mitotic exit by facilitating the binding of TEMP1 to CDC15. Also involved in the pathway that organizes the shaping and sizing of the prospore membrane (PSM) during sporulation. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11101520}.

FUNCTION: Functions in nuclear protein import as nuclear transport receptor. Serves as receptor for classical and arginine/glycine-rich nuclear localization signals (cNLS and rg-NLS) in cargo substrates (PubMed:15367670). Its predominant cargo substrate seems to be ribosomal proteins and ribosome biogenesis trans- and cis-acting factors (PubMed:15367670, PubMed:9182759, PubMed:9321403). Required for nuclear transport of YAP1, NOP1 and SOF1 (PubMed:11274141, PubMed:15367670). Mediates the nuclear import of histones H3 and H4 (PubMed:11694505). Mediates docking of the importin/substrate complex to the nuclear pore complex (NPC) through binding to repeat-containing nucleoporins. The complex is subsequently translocated through the pore by an energy requiring, Ran-dependent mechanism (PubMed:11423015). At the nucleoplasmic side of the NPC, GTP-Ran binding leads to release of the cargo (PubMed:9321403). The importin is re-exported from the nucleus to the cytoplasm where GTP hydrolysis releases Ran from importin. The directionality of nuclear import is thought to be conferred by an asymmetric distribution of the GTP- and GDP-bound forms of Ran between the cytoplasm and nucleus (PubMed:11423015). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11274141, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11694505, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15367670, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9182759, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9321403, ECO:0000305|PubMed:11423015}.; FUNCTION: Plays a role in protein secretion. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:1522152}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: C-8 sterol isomerase; part of the third module of ergosterol biosynthesis pathway that includes the late steps of the pathway (Ref.5). ERG2 catalyzes the reaction which results in unsaturation at C-7 in the B ring of sterols and thus converts fecosterol to episterol (Ref.5). The third module or late pathway involves the ergosterol synthesis itself through consecutive reactions that mainly occur in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane. Firstly, the squalene synthase ERG9 catalyzes the condensation of 2 farnesyl pyrophosphate moieties to form squalene, which is the precursor of all steroids. Squalene synthase is crucial for balancing the incorporation of farnesyl diphosphate (FPP) into sterol and nonsterol isoprene synthesis. Secondly, the squalene epoxidase ERG1 catalyzes the stereospecific oxidation of squalene to (S)-2,3-epoxysqualene, which is considered to be a rate-limiting enzyme in steroid biosynthesis. Then, the lanosterol synthase ERG7 catalyzes the cyclization of (S)-2,3 oxidosqualene to lanosterol, a reaction that forms the sterol core. In the next steps, lanosterol is transformed to zymosterol through a complex process involving various demethylation, reduction and desaturation reactions. The lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase ERG11 (also known as CYP51) catalyzes C14-demethylation of lanosterol to produce 4,4'-dimethyl cholesta-8,14,24-triene-3-beta-ol, which is critical for ergosterol biosynthesis. The C-14 reductase ERG24 reduces the C14=C15 double bond of 4,4-dimethyl-cholesta-8,14,24-trienol to produce 4,4-dimethyl-cholesta-8,24-dienol. 4,4-dimethyl-cholesta-8,24-dienol is substrate of the C-4 demethylation complex ERG25-ERG26-ERG27 in which ERG25 catalyzes the three-step monooxygenation required for the demethylation of 4,4-dimethyl and 4alpha-methylsterols, ERG26 catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation that results in a reduction of the 3-beta-hydroxy group at the C-3 carbon to an oxo group, and ERG27 is responsible for the reduction of the keto group on the C-3. ERG28 has a role as a scaffold to help anchor ERG25, ERG26 and ERG27 to the endoplasmic reticulum and ERG29 regulates the activity of the iron-containing C4-methylsterol oxidase ERG25. Then, the sterol 24-C-methyltransferase ERG6 catalyzes the methyl transfer from S-adenosyl-methionine to the C-24 of zymosterol to form fecosterol. The C-8 sterol isomerase ERG2 catalyzes the reaction which results in unsaturation at C-7 in the B ring of sterols and thus converts fecosterol to episterol. The sterol-C5-desaturase ERG3 then catalyzes the introduction of a C-5 double bond in the B ring to produce 5-dehydroepisterol. The C-22 sterol desaturase ERG5 further converts 5-dehydroepisterol into ergosta-5,7,22,24(28)-tetraen-3beta-ol by forming the C-22(23) double bond in the sterol side chain. Finally, ergosta-5,7,22,24(28)-tetraen-3beta-ol is substrate of the C-24(28) sterol reductase ERG4 to produce ergosterol (PubMed:32679672). {ECO:0000269|Ref.5, ECO:0000303|PubMed:32679672}.

Part of the tauA domain of TFIIIC that binds boxA DNA promoter sites of tRNA and similar genes. Participates in the interconnection of tauA with tauB via its contacts with TFC3 and TFC6. Serves as a scaffold critical for tauA-DNA spatial configuration and tauB-DNA stability. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:12533520, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7688737}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Septins are GTPases involved in cytokinesis that assemble early in the cell cycle as a patch at the incipient bud site and form a ring approximate 15 minutes before bud emergence, which transforms into an hour-glass shaped collar of cortical filaments that spans both sides of the mother-bud neck. FUNCTION: Delta(14)-sterol reductase; part of the third module of ergosterol biosynthesis pathway that includes the late steps of the pathway (PubMed:1418625, PubMed:8125337). ERG24 reduces the C14=C15 double bond of 4,4-dimethyl-cholesta-8,14,24-trienol to produce 4,4-dimethyl-cholesta-8,24-dienol (PubMed:1418625, PubMed:8125337). The third module or late pathway involves the ergosterol synthesis itself through consecutive reactions that mainly occur in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane. Firstly, the squalene synthase ERG9 catalyzes the condensation of 2 farnesyl pyrophosphate moieties to form squalene, which is the precursor of all steroids. Squalene synthase is crucial for balancing the incorporation of farnesyl diphosphate (FPP) into sterol and nonsterol isoprene synthesis. Secondly, the squalene epoxidase ERG1 catalyzes the stereospecific oxidation of squalene to (S)-2,3-epoxysqualene, which is considered to be a rate-limiting enzyme in steroid biosynthesis. Then, the lanosterol synthase ERG7 catalyzes the cyclization of (S)-2,3 oxidosqualene to lanosterol, a reaction that forms the sterol core. In the next steps, lanosterol is transformed to zymosterol through a complex process involving various demethylation, reduction and desaturation reactions. The lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase ERG11 (also known as CYP51) catalyzes C14-demethylation of lanosterol to produce 4,4'-dimethyl cholesta-8,14,24-triene-3-beta-ol, which is critical for ergosterol biosynthesis. The C-14 reductase ERG24 reduces the C14=C15 double bond of 4,4-dimethyl-cholesta-8,14,24-trienol to produce 4,4-dimethyl-cholesta-8,24-dienol. 4,4-dimethyl-cholesta-8,24-dienol is substrate of the C-4 demethylation complex ERG25-ERG26-ERG27 in which ERG25 catalyzes the three-step monooxygenation required for the demethylation of 4,4-dimethyl and 4alpha-methylsterols, ERG26 catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation that results in a reduction of the 3-beta-hydroxy group at the C-3 carbon to an oxo group, and ERG27 is responsible for the reduction of the keto group on the C-3. ERG28 has a role as a scaffold to help anchor ERG25, ERG26 and ERG27 to the endoplasmic reticulum and ERG29 regulates the activity of the iron-containing C4-methylsterol oxidase ERG25. Then, the sterol 24-C-methyltransferase ERG6 catalyzes the methyl transfer from S-adenosyl-methionine to the C-24 of zymosterol to form fecosterol. The C-8 sterol isomerase ERG2 catalyzes the reaction which results in unsaturation at C-7 in the B ring of sterols and thus converts fecosterol to episterol. The sterol-C5-desaturase ERG3 then catalyzes the introduction of a C-5 double bond in the B ring to produce 5-dehydroepisterol. The C-22 sterol desaturase ERG5 further converts 5-dehydroepisterol into ergosta-5,7,22,24(28)-tetraen-3beta-ol by forming the C-22(23) double bond in the sterol side chain. Finally, ergosta-5,7,22,24(28)-tetraen-3beta-ol is substrate of the C-24(28) sterol reductase ERG4 to produce ergosterol (PubMed:32679672). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:1418625, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8125337, ECO:0000303|PubMed:32679672}.
